anagramAllIntroDesc:
One set of letters and every word it makes. Empty cells show how long each word is.

🎚 Levels: from 6 to 22 targets — that is the difficulty. A six-word layout is a minute; eighteen is a sitting. No time limit.

⚠️ A word outside the target list is not a mistake: it counts as a bonus if it exists in the dictionary.

The hint opens one word, Shuffle reorders the letters.
anagramClassicIntroDesc:
One word is hidden, its letters shuffled around a ring. Rebuild it by tapping the letters in order.

🎚 Levels: the word grows from 4 letters to 9 (L1–L11); above that it is not length that grows but haste — from L7 each word is timed, down to 15 seconds.

⚠️ ANY word of that length made from the same letters counts, not just the hidden one: one set of letters usually yields several.

The hint opens the next letter, Shuffle reorders the ring, ten words per round.
anagramCrossIntroDesc:
Words from one set of letters fill a grid and cross each other. An open letter is half of its neighbour — you see it at the crossing.

🎚 Levels: from 6 to 10 words in the grid; hints start at 5 and shrink as levels rise.

⚠️ Order is free: start from any word, the crossings will give you the rest.
anagramSquareIntroDesc:
Four words along the edges of a square, all from one pool of letters. Neighbouring words share a corner letter — place it in one and it lands in the other.

🎚 Levels: the square side stays 5 letters; what grows is the number of near-misses — letters that almost make a word.

⚠️ You answer by dragging across letters; there is no submit button — a word counts as soon as it is assembled.
anagramsDesc: Make words from shuffled letters — four modes
anagramsIntroDesc:
One pile of shuffled letters becomes words. The letters come from the theme and language you pick; they grow longer and more numerous as levels rise.

🎛 Modes — chosen before the round:
• Classic — rebuild the one hidden word
• All words — find every word the letters hide: empty cells show how long each one is
• Crossword — words cross in a grid, and an open letter gives away its neighbour
• Word square — four words along the edges, sharing their corner letters

Trains vocabulary, mental flexibility and the knack of seeing structure in chaos.
animalQueueDesc: Line the animals up by the clues, starting from the door 🚪. 🦁 ➜ 🦊: the lion is somewhere ahead of the fox; 🦁 🔗 🦊: the fox is right behind the lion
antIntroDesc: Look at the centre. First a cue flashes — to one side, in the middle, in two places at once, or not at all. Then a row of arrows appears: press the way the MIDDLE one points. The neighbours often point elsewhere and throw you off — ignore them. The game catches three separate things at once: whether the cue got you ready, whether it helped you find the place, and how much the neighbours interfere. The Fan–Posner test, 2002.
antLvlParams: {n} trials · ~{p}% conflict · {w} s response window · less predictable pauses
aqClueApart: {a} and {b} do not stand side by side
attentionConflictFootnote: One theme here: holding a rule while everything pushes you to answer otherwise. The interference comes in different shapes — a conflicting feature, a forbidden ready move, a habit that costs you — and each paradigm keeps its own measure.
attentionConflictIntroDesc:
This is not an exercise but a fork: the card opens a group of tests on suppressing an automatic response.

They share one thing — the correct answer competes with the one that suggests itself. Reading a word is easier than naming the colour it is printed in. Pressing everything is easier than holding back at the right moment. What gets trained is exactly that gap between the easy move and the right one. Pick the test you want inside.
backupRestoredMsg: Restored {n} records. Restart the app to apply the data.
ballSortDesc: Sort balls into tubes: one colour per tube
ballSortIntroDesc: Tap a tube to lift its top run of one colour, tap another to roll them across. You may only roll onto the same colour or into an empty tube, and only while there is room. The level is done when every tube is empty or full of one colour. Think ahead about where the colour in your way will go: there are only two free tubes.
bartIntroDesc: Each press pumps the balloon and puts a coin in the pot, but the pot is not yours yet. Press "Collect" and the money goes to the bank. The balloon can burst, and every balloon has its own limit, which you cannot see in advance. If it bursts, the pot is gone; the bank stays. The whole game is about where to stop: play it too safe and you earn little, push too far and you lose what you gathered.
bartPass: To pass: reasonable avg pumps without frequent bursts
bilingualModeDesc: {a} and {b} mixed together, your own language stays the anchor. Expect more mistakes — that is the point
bossIntroFinderror: Find the ERROR — a repeat in a row
bossIntroOddletter: Find the ODD letter — the vowel
brTechSighDesc: Double inhale + long exhale — fast reset
brWimHoldHint: Exhale and hold. Tap when you need to breathe.
brWimWarnBody: The Wim Hof method is hyperventilation with breath holds. Do it ONLY while sitting or lying down. NEVER while driving, in water, or if pregnant, epileptic, or with heart conditions. If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.
breathingIntroDesc: Breathing techniques for relaxation, focus and recovery. An animated circle sets the rhythm: it grows on inhale, shrinks on exhale. Vibration cues each phase change.
cakeSortDesc: Gather a circle of six matching slices
cakeSortIntroDesc: Drag a cake slice from one plate to another — or tap the slice, then the plate. A slice only goes onto its own flavour or onto an empty spot. Complete a full circle of six matching slices and the plate leaves, freeing the spot. Some plates wait in a queue and come out by themselves as soon as a spot opens: the queue is finite and shown in the header. That is the whole task — free up space in good time instead of piling a mix onto every plate.
catsDesc: Place one cat in every row, every column and every colour. Cats may not touch — not even diagonally.
catsHowPress: Long press reveals a cat; a short tap marks ✕
catsRuleLine: One cat per row and column
catsRuleTouch: Cats may not touch, not even diagonally
catsWhyColumn: Only one square left in this column
catsWhyRegion: Only one square left in this colour
catsWhyRow: Only one square left in this row
catsWhyTrial: No forced move — search from here
chessAssistBoard: Show an empty board during questions
chessAssistNote: With the board this is no longer mental work: colour and position are visible. Use it while you are still learning the coordinates.
chessBlindConfigDesc: Memorize a position from a real game — the pieces get masked as identical tokens. Keep track of what each token is, even as they move.
chessBlindDesc: Board visualization trainer: squares, knight, memory
chessBlindIntroDesc: TWO MODES. A series of three tasks on ONE position from a real game: first compare two squares by colour, then tell whether a knight gets from one to the other in N moves, then whether a named piece stood on a square. The time difference between tasks shows what it costs you to apply the move rule, and what it costs to hold the position in your head. There is no board on screen during the questions: it lives in your head, otherwise this is not a measurement. The second mode is a game: a position from a real puzzle is shown for a few seconds, then the pieces turn into identical tokens and move blindfolded. ⚠️ This is a board visualization trainer, not a reproduction of a scientific paradigm: positions come from an offline sample of real puzzles (Lichess, public domain), and the time difference is the cost of one added rule in this game on this position, nothing beyond that.
chessGroupDesc: Board, squares and pieces: hold the position in your head and recognise the pattern
chessGroupFootnote: One board, two skills. Board in Mind takes the position out of sight and measures what you held. Scholar’s Mate leaves it in plain sight and measures how many seconds it takes you to spot a familiar pattern.
chessGroupIntroDesc:
Two chess exercises, and they train DIFFERENT things — which is why there are two of them rather than one with a toggle.

Board in Mind takes the position out of sight: square colours, knight routes, position recall and a blindfold game. What is measured is how much you held without a board in front of you.

Scholar’s Mate leaves the position in plain sight and starts a stopwatch. The pattern is always the same — queen and bishop on f7 — you already KNOW it, and the question is not whether you can but how fast you see it. Time per position shrinks from 20 seconds to 4, and from level 31 on comes mate with a SACRIFICE in two or three moves.

Positions come from two sources: an in-house generator of classic opening traps and the Lichess puzzle database (CC0) — real scholar’s mates from played games, picked by rating.
chessHintWhereIs: Where is the {piece} {glyph}? Tap the square
chineseTonesDesc: Hear a syllable, name its tone
chineseTonesIntroDesc:
One Chinese syllable is played. You answer which tone it carried: level, rising, dipping, or falling. Later you also pick the syllable itself from four spellings.

In Chinese the tone is not decoration but part of the word: mā is “mother”, mà is “to scold” — the same syllable. For an ear raised on a non-tonal language this is the most alien part of the language: pitch there carries the melody of a sentence, not the meaning of a word, and at first the brain simply does not hear the difference. Here it is taken apart one syllable at a time, until it becomes audible on its own.
choiceRtHint: When an arrow appears, press the button on the same side
choiceRtIntroDesc: An arrow ←, →, ↑ or ↓ appears. Tap the matching direction button as fast as you can. Trains choice speed and motor accuracy.
clozeIntroDesc: A sentence in the target language with a gap — pick the word that fits. Grammar and meaning are tested together: distractors come from the same semantic category, so you can’t guess by form. Trains word retrieval in real context — the way words are actually used in speech.
clozePass: To pass: ≥80% correct answers (running out of time counts as an error)
colorblindWhere: Applies where colour carries meaning: Sudoku, SET, Stroop, Wisconsin test, Tower of London
comingSoonBody:
This profile will open after launch. Available free right now:
💊 NZT-48 · 🌸 Micro-relax · 🧒 Kids · 👴 50+ · 🎓 Students
— pick any of them.
corsiIntroDesc: A board with 9 blocks. They light up in sequence — memorize the order. Then reproduce it (or in reverse). Length grows until you fail twice. Classic visuospatial working memory test.
counterHint: Tap numbers until they add up to the target
counterIntroDesc: Tap numbers in the grid until they add up to the target. Find numbers that sum to the target. Trains mental arithmetic and the ability to quickly analyze options.
countingGroupDesc: Numbers in the head: counting, estimating, speed
countingGroupFootnote: Different takes on one skill: hold a number, estimate, count fast, split into parts, continue a series.
countingGroupIntroDesc:
Four takes on one skill. Counter holds a number while new ones are added; Slider asks you to estimate without computing; Sprint pushes simple sums for speed; Bonds split a number into parts.

Mental arithmetic is not really about arithmetic. It rests on working memory: you must hold an intermediate result while computing the next step. That is why counting degrades with fatigue earlier than reading or speech — and why it shows what shape you are in.
cptDesc: Tap X. On higher levels — only when X follows A
cptIntroDesc: About once a second a letter appears. On the first levels, press every X. Later the rule gets stricter: press only the X that had an A before it, and let the rest go. The pace picks up and letters that look like X get mixed in. A round always runs about 90 seconds: it is the task that gets harder, not the clock. The hard part is not the start but the end — attention sags in the last minutes for everyone, and that is exactly what the game is watching.

cptLvlParamsAXHard: AX-CPT · X after A · faster + look-alikes · 90 s

cptLvlParamsLetter: AX-CPT · tap {letter} only after A · look-alikes · 90 s

cptTapColor: Only a RED {letter} after A. Ignore other colours
ctConfigDesc: In Chinese the tone is the meaning: mā “mother”, mà “to scold”. A syllable is played — you name its tone. Later, the whole syllable.
deepDesc: Sudoku inside sudoku inside sudoku — a marathon into the deep
deepDiveHint: A dashed cell is a door into a nested sudoku: tap to dive in
deepHowTo: The first grid is the top. Dashed cells hide their own sudokus: dive down to the bottom, solve the leaves — digits float up. Finish the root grid to win. The game is long and saves itself: come back anytime.
deepLeafHint: This is the bottom. Solve the grid to its threshold — the centre digit floats up
deepPortalHint: Portal: this cell holds the same digit as cell {cell} of a sibling board on this layer
deepPresetDesc_abyss: 3 layers, a puzzle under every empty cell — a weeks-long marathon
deepPresetDesc_scout: 2 layers, nine lower grids — a taste of the mechanic
deepPresetDesc_trek: 3 layers, twelve grids per node — several evenings
desc_counter_rules: Select numbers that sum to the target. If sum exceeds target - error!
desc_full_library: Full library: 12 memory · 7 attention · 14 logic · 15 speed/inhibition. All 48 — no limits.
desc_photo_memory: All cards flash for an instant — memorize them and match the pairs
desc_profile_section: Each profile has its own set of exercises, its own warm-up playlist and its own history.
desc_word_pairs_rules: Memorize word pairs, then restore connections. Penalty: 15 sec per error.
dictationConfigDesc: The phrase is spoken but not shown. Type it by ear: a typo blocks the way, and you may replay as often as you like.
dictationDesc: A phrase is read out — you type it in full
dictationHint: Untyped characters stay dotted — this is dictation, not copying
dictationIntroDesc:
The phrase is spoken but not shown — untyped characters stay dotted. You type what you heard in full, and a typo holds the cursor until the right key is pressed. Replay as often as you like: that is the task being delivered, not a hint.

The point is not typing speed. Reading and typing run at different speeds, and the fast channel outruns the slow one — the eye races ahead, the hand lags, attention tears. Dictation brings them together by SLOWING the fast one: the voice sets the pace and the hand must keep up without dropping anything. The result shows characters per minute, accuracy, and your weak keys — the letters you stumble on most.
dictationNeedsKeyboard: A real keyboard is required: the exercise matches listening speed to typing speed, and on an on-screen keyboard that is a different task.
digitSpanIntroDesc: Digits appear one by one — type them in order (or backward). Classic neuropsych short-term memory test.
dotsConnectDesc: Connect matching dots with non-crossing paths and fill the whole grid
dotsConnectIntroDesc: Drag your finger from a dot to its partner of the same colour — a path follows your finger. Paths of different pairs never cross, and by the end no cell may stay empty. Trains spatial planning.
exitConfirmLost: This game will not be saved: the board and your progress will be lost.
exitConfirmSaved: Your game will be saved — come back and pick up where you left off.
exportCodeHint: Copy this code and paste it into "Import" on another device.
eyeDisclaimer: Relieves screen eye-strain. It does not cure vision or replace an eye exam.
eyeFocusSub: Look at a distant object, not the screen
eyeGymDesc: Warm up and unstrain your eyes from the screen
eyeGymIntroDesc: A set of exercises: follow the moving dot, shift focus into the distance and converge your gaze. Relieves screen eye-strain. Follow the dot with your eyes, without moving your head.
eyeInstrConverge: Keep both eyes on the approaching dot
eyeInstrFocusFar: Look away — focus far into the distance (a window, ~6 m)
eyeInstrPalming: Cover your eyes with your palms, relax and blink
eyeInstrPulse: The dot shrinks and grows — keep it sharp
eyeInstrPursuit: Follow the dot with your eyes, keep your head still
eyeInstrSpiral: The dot spirals — follow it, do not cut corners
eyeInstrWarmup: Follow the dot in each direction
eyeInstrWave: A wave: the path is not straight, do not predict it
eyePalmBlink: Relax your eyes and blink slowly
eyeStereoComfort: Do not strain your eyes. If it is uncomfortable or you cannot see a shape, skip it. This is not a vision test or treatment.
eyeStereoInstruction: Look through the pattern — find the 3D shape.
eyeStereoOptional: Optional optical puzzle: it is not part of levels and does not affect eye-gym results.
facesNamesDesc: Link a face to a name and a fact
facesNamesIntroDesc: Associative memory: remember a procedural portrait, an exact name, and a fact about the person, then recall each part separately. This is the everyday failure “I know the face but not the name”: recognising a face and retrieving the word attached to it are different abilities, and the second one goes first.
findDiffDesc: Spot what differs between two scenes
findDiffIntroDesc: Tap the differences on the lower picture. Find every difference between the two scenes. Trains detail attention and visual comparison.
findMoveDesc: A position from a real game: find the move that wins — a mate, a piece or a decisive blow. Twelve tactical motifs, from a hanging piece to mate in two.
findMoveThemesOpen: The motif is not named — recognise it yourself
flankerIntroDesc: Center: an arrow ← or →. Sides: distractor flankers (same or opposite direction). Respond only to the CENTER, ignoring the sides. Measures ability to suppress automatic responses (Eriksen Flanker, 1974).
flankerLvlParams: {p}% conflict arrows · {w} s response window · 20 trials
fractalDesc: Behind every cell of the top grid hides a whole sudoku
fractalPortalHint: A ringed cell is one and the same cell in two grids at once. Neither grid names its digit alone: narrow the candidates here, narrow them there, and the answer is what both allow.
fractalRedDigit: A red digit is a mistake: the same one already stands in this row, column or box. It stays on the board so you can see what to fix.
fractalSolutionAskAll: Show the answer to the whole sudoku? The game ends as a review: the level won't count, but it won't drop either.
fractalSolutionAskChild: Show the answer to this lower grid? The level won't count for this game, but it won't drop either.
fractalSolutionUsed: Solution shown — the level won't count for this game.
fractalTitleIntroDesc:
Behind every cell of the top grid hides a whole sudoku. Solve the nested one and its answer becomes the digit in that cell above.

You are solving on two levels at once. The top grid tells you which digit is needed below; the nested one tells you whether that digit can be reached there at all. When those two answers disagree, you go back and redo the lower grid.
fractalUndecided: This cell is not decided yet: the digit breaks no rule, but it does not follow either. That is not a mistake — resolve the portal first.
goNoGoDesc: Tap on green, hold on red
goNoGoIntroDesc: Tap as fast as you can on the green stimulus. Do NOT tap on red. A standard neuropsych test for inhibitory control.
goodsSortDesc: Group three identical goods on a shelf
goodsSortIntroDesc: Drag a good into a niche — or tap it, then the niche. Three identical goods in one niche vanish. Each level states its own goal above the cabinet: clear everything, gather the named goods, stay within the move limit, or free the flagged niches. Later come obstacles — locked niches, timed locks, covered goods, a frozen row. A niche holds three, so a pair blocks it until the third turns up: think about where you put things, not just what.
hanoiDesc: Move all discs to the right peg
hanoiIntroDesc: Move the tower of discs from the left peg to the right one. A larger disc may never sit on a smaller one. Trains planning, recursion and problem solving.
hcStart: Ask a question — those who do not match will fade
hcWrong: Not them — the hidden one is outlined in green
hearingGroupDesc: The task is heard: tell apart, repeat, name the tone
hearingGroupFootnote: Most of them need a system voice: without one the exercise says so instead of pretending. Rhythm and pitch need none — those are tones.
hearingGroupIntroDesc:
Three exercises where the task is HEARD, not written. Minimal pairs teach you to hear the difference between close foreign sounds; Chinese tones train the melody of a syllable that carries the meaning; pseudoword echo measures how much sound you can hold in your head.

Your native language mutes foreign sounds: the ones it lacks get bent into familiar shapes until you stop hearing the difference. All three bring that difference back.
hiddenCharacterDesc: One of the characters is hiding. Ask about features — “Hat?”, “Glasses?” — and those who do not match fade out. When you are sure, pick a character and press “That’s the one!”. The fewer questions, the better.
hint_center_arrow: Answer by the CENTRE arrow — the side ones mislead
hint_profile_tap_unlock: Tap a profile → details and unlock with a code
hint_simon_color_rule: 🔵 → ⬅️ left  ·  🔴 → ➡️ right  (by color, not by position)
hint_top_to_bottom: Top to bottom, left to right
importDoneMsg: Imported {n} entries. Restart the app to see your progress.
importFailedBody: Code is invalid or empty. Copy it fully.
inhibPass: To pass: ≥80% correct (pressing on NO/stop or missing GO counts as an error)
inhibStopLvlParams: {n} trials · {w} s window · ~{p}% stop trials · stop at {d} ms
inhibitionDesc: Go/No-Go and Stop-Signal in one game
inhibitionGngHint: Green = press. Red = DON'T press. Decide before moving.
inhibitionIntroDesc: Two different kinds of stopping in one game. "Hold back" — decide NOT to press before your hand moves. "Cancel" — stop a press you have already started, on a sudden signal; this is harder, and misses here are normal. "Mix" alternates the two, and switching between them is harder than doing either alone. Each mode is scored separately, so earlier rounds do not get mixed up with new ones.
inhibitionMixedHint: Alternates Go/No-Go and Stop-Signal — trains switching between inhibition types.
inhibitionSsHint: Tap GO fast. If ✋ appears — cancel the initiated motion.
iowaHint: Pick a deck · Learn which are good
iowaIntroDesc: Four decks in front of you. Every card brings a win, and sometimes a loss along with it. Two decks look more generous but occasionally hit hard enough to eat everything you earned; the other two give less and stay ahead over the long run. Which is which is not stated — you find out as you go, from your own losses. The goal is simple: finish the round in the black. The Iowa Gambling Task.
kidsFindDesc: One shape on the board is not like the others — tap it. There is no sample: you find it by comparing the shapes with each other. First it differs in colour, then in shape, then in size; later the other shapes are mixed too, and then the odd one differs only by a combination of colour and shape. Five boards per level, one mistake is allowed.
kidsSortDesc: Put each card in the matching box. First by colour; then the rule changes without warning — find the new one from ✓ and ✗
knightsQueensDesc: Two classic puzzles on one board. Eight Queens: place the queens so that none attacks another. Knight’s Tour: lead the knight over every square, each exactly once. Each mode has its own 24-step ladder: from small boards up to 8×8 with holes, obstacles and a single solution.
kqMistakeUnknown: Could not find the mistake — try Undo
kqNoMistake: No mistake: a solution still exists from here
kqQueensAbout: Tap to place a queen, tap again to remove it. Dark queens are given and stay put; squares with a cross are off limits.
kqQueensRule: Place {n} queens — none may attack another
kqQueensStuck: The queens attack each other — rearrange them
kqTourAbout: Tap a dotted square to jump the knight there. Visited squares are numbered. If there is a flag, finish on it.
kqTourRule: Visit every square with the knight, each once
kqTourRuleEnd: Visit every square and finish on the flag
label_themed_codes_off: 🎯 Themed · 5 free now, the rest coming soon
languagesGroupDesc: Memory for a word and memory for how it sounds
languagesGroupFootnote: The two sides of a foreign language train differently: vocabulary by eye, pronunciation by ear. Hence two doors rather than one flat list.
languagesGroupIntroDesc:
A foreign language rests on two different memories. One is for the word: recognising it, recalling it unaided, pulling it out in a second. The other is for sound: hearing the difference between close phonemes, holding it, reproducing it.

Neither replaces the other. You can know a thousand words and not follow fluent speech; you can polish pronunciation and have nothing to say. Hence two doors: Words and Hearing.
lexicalDecisionIntroDesc: The classic lexical decision task: a string in the target language appears — a real word or a plausible fake (one or two letters swapped). Decide as fast as you can. Speed and accuracy reflect how quickly words are retrieved from your mental lexicon — the key marker of language automaticity. For Chinese, a “non-word” is a character combination not present in the training dictionary.
listeningSpanDesc: Hear the words — repeat the order
listeningSpanIntroDesc:
You hear a list of words and repeat it in the same order. Each level makes the list longer.

This is the auditory version of memory span, and it is harder than the visual one: a picture can be "photographed" in the mind, sound is gone the instant it ends. It trains working memory in the form it actually works in — in meetings, in lectures, in a conversation in a foreign language.
lr_animal_queue_apart_example: Example: the lion has just taken spot 2, so the bear cannot take spot 3.
lr_animal_queue_apart_rule: A new clue: 🦁 🚫 🐻 means the lion and the bear do not stand next to each other: someone stands between them. Which of them is ahead is not said.
lr_animal_queue_glued_example: Example: 🚪 🦉 and 🦉 🔗 🐻: the owl is first, the bear second.
lr_animal_queue_glued_rule: The queue starts at the door 🚪. The clue 🚪 🦁 means the lion stands first. 🦁 🔗 🦊 means the fox stands right behind the lion, with nobody in between. 🦁 ➜ 🦊 means only that the lion is somewhere ahead.
lr_animal_queue_last_example: Example: four animals and 🐟 🏁: the fish takes spot 4.
lr_animal_queue_last_rule: A new clue: 🦊 🏁 means the fox stands at the very end of the queue. Do not place it before the last spot.
lr_ball_sort_hidden_example: Example: a “?” sits under the blue ball. Roll the blue one away and it opens: a yellow ball was hiding there.
lr_ball_sort_hidden_rule: One ball in a tube is covered by a question mark — it has a colour, but you cannot see it. It opens by itself once nothing is left above it. Such a level has no move minimum: scouting costs moves. Roll, find out and replan — undo is free.
lr_ball_sort_movelimit_example: Example: the limit is 40 and you have used 38 — two moves left to roll the rest home. Not enough means the level restarts with the same tubes.
lr_ball_sort_movelimit_rule: From this level the round has a move limit, shown at the top. It has slack: roughly a quarter of the moves above flawless play is left for changing your mind. Undo does NOT give a move back: change your mind and you have spent it. Levels with hidden balls have no limit — scouting costs moves there.
lr_ball_sort_movelimit_title: A move limit for the balls
lr_ball_sort_sealed_example: Example: the lock lifts once the first colour is done. So the first colour must be finished without this tube.
lr_ball_sort_sealed_rule: One tube is locked: balls can neither roll in nor roll out until you have completed enough colours. The lock lifts by itself — it counts finished COLOURS, not moves. Until then you have to manage with the other tubes.
lr_ball_sort_short_example: Example: a tube that holds three balls. There are five red ones, so this tube cannot be their home.
lr_ball_sort_short_rule: One tube is shorter than the rest — it holds fewer balls. It still counts as a full home: a colour completed there is finished like anywhere else. But a colour of five balls will not fit into a tube for four — take it elsewhere, or split it and gather it later.
lr_ball_sort_stones_example: Example: you park the blue balls there to reach the yellow ones below. Before you finish, those blue balls have to roll back out.
lr_ball_sort_stones_rule: One tube has stones on its floor — they cannot be moved. You may roll balls into it, and that is its whole purpose: temporary storage. But it will never become a colour’s home, and the level only comes together once it is empty again.
lr_cake_sort_queue_example: Example: the queue shows 2. You complete a circle, the plate leaves, and the first one from the queue takes its place at once.
lr_cake_sort_queue_rule: Some plates wait their turn and come out by themselves — as soon as a spot frees up, that is, when you complete a circle. The queue is finite and shown in the header: it is not an endless stream but a delayed part of this very level. So free up space in good time instead of piling a mix onto every plate.
lr_chess_blind_locate_example: Holding the position as "square → piece" stops working. You need the reverse list: "piece → square".
lr_chess_blind_locate_rule: It used to ask "what stands on this square" — you checked one place. Now it asks "where does this piece stand", and you have to search the whole board.
lr_chess_blind_moves_example: Example: "knight b1 to c3". Move it in your head and remember the new square; the old one no longer counts.
lr_chess_blind_moves_rule: Up to level 5 the position froze and remembering the picture was enough. From level 6 the pieces make blind moves after the display — and what you must hold is not the picture but how it changed.
lr_corsi_hold_example: The blocks have finished flashing, the board stays quiet for a couple of seconds — only then can you tap.
lr_corsi_hold_rule: From this level a pause appears between the last flash and your input, and it grows further on. You have to hold the sequence in mind for longer — the length and the pace of the flashes stay the same.
lr_corsi_reverse_rule: From this level on, reproduce the sequence in REVERSE — from the last block back to the first.
lr_counter_triples_rule: From this level the target may be built from THREE cells, not just two. No pair works — look for a triple.
lr_cpt_colorrule_example: Example: the target in red — tap. The same letter in blue — let it pass.
lr_cpt_colorrule_rule: Now only a RED target counts. The same letter in another colour is a trap — don't tap it.
lr_cpt_colorrule_title: Colour is part of the rule
lr_cpt_lookalike_example: Example: a K flashes by — hands off, it's not an X.
lr_cpt_lookalike_rule: Letters that resemble X now appear more often: K, Y, V, W, N, M. Don't tap them — wait for a real X (after A).
lr_cpt_newtarget_example: Example: if the hint says tap K, then X is just another letter — let it pass.
lr_cpt_newtarget_rule: From this level the target is no longer X. The letter you need is named in the hint above the field, and it changes from level to level.
lr_digit_span_reverse_rule: From this level on, enter the digits in REVERSE order — last digit first.
lr_digit_span_surprise_dir_example: You saw 5-2-8-1, and only now it says "ascending" — the answer is 1-2-5-8.
lr_digit_span_surprise_dir_rule: From this level you learn HOW to give the row back only after it is shown: forward, backward or in ascending order. Hold it as you saw it until you are asked.
lr_goods_sort_backrow_example: Example: the niche looked empty after the last item — and three more stepped out from behind. They were there all along, just out of sight.
lr_goods_sort_backrow_rule: Some niches have a back row: goods that are not on the board yet. The niche looks shorter than it is, and the back row takes no space until it comes forward. Clear the front row completely and the back one steps into its place. Everything there was counted into the task from the start — nothing extra appears.
lr_goods_sort_blocked_example: Example: 🔒 in the corner. Clear a triple in the adjacent niche and the lock falls off.
lr_goods_sort_blocked_rule: A niche with a padlock is shut — nothing goes in. It opens by itself once a triple clears next to it, so free the neighbours.
lr_goods_sort_collapse_example: Example: you lined up a cola for the niche above the finished one — the shelf left and what stood higher took its place. Nothing vanished; the address changed.
lr_goods_sort_collapse_rule: Complete a triple in a three-slot niche and the shelf closes and leaves the cabinet. Everything above it in that column settles down, and a new shelf arrives from the queue at the top. The queue is finite: as many shelves as it holds will arrive, and everything on them was counted into the task from the start. A four-slot niche does not close — there the triple forms next to a fourth item, and that item is not going anywhere.
lr_goods_sort_covered_example: Example: a black shape behind the cola. Move the cola and kefir appears.
lr_goods_sort_covered_rule: A dark silhouette is a good you cannot see yet. It is never the front one: take the item in front of it and you will find out what it is.
lr_goods_sort_frozen_example: Example: ❄ the bottom row is frozen on juice. Clear a triple of juice anywhere and it thaws.
lr_goods_sort_frozen_rule: A blue row is out of action — nothing in, nothing out. It thaws when you clear a triple of the frozen good, shown by the snowflake.
lr_goods_sort_goalfree_example: Example: 🚩 two flags. Empty both niches and the level is done.
lr_goods_sort_goalfree_rule: Flagged niches must end up empty — move everything out of them. Whatever sits elsewhere does not matter for this goal.
lr_goods_sort_goalpick_example: Example: 🚩 Gather triples of: milk, cola. Clear both and the level is done, even with kefir still there.
lr_goods_sort_goalpick_rule: Levels now carry their own goal, written above the cabinet. “Gather triples” means clearing exactly the goods shown — the rest may stay on the shelves.
lr_goods_sort_hidden_example: Example: a niche holds “?” and a cola. Move the cola and the “?” opens: it was kefir.
lr_goods_sort_hidden_rule: What sits deep in a niche is unknown — it shows as “?”. A good opens up once nothing stands in front of it. No move minimum exists here, so the move count is not judged — uncover, learn, replan.
lr_goods_sort_joker_example: Example: ★ is empty, a cola sits on top and no other cola is left. Park it in the wildcard and you free the niche for a triple of kefir.
lr_goods_sort_joker_rule: One niche is marked with a star: any good may go into it, even while strict stacking is in force. It adds no room — it holds as much as the others; what it lifts is the ban, not the crowding. Keep it empty until you are stuck: it is your only sideways move.
lr_goods_sort_locked_example: Example: ⏱ 5 — opens in five of your moves. Every move takes one off.
lr_goods_sort_locked_rule: A niche with a clock opens by itself after as many moves as the counter shows. No need to wait for it — just treat it as taken while it counts down.
lr_goods_sort_mixedcap_example: Example: two notches under a niche means room for two goods only. A third will not go in, even if it matches.
lr_goods_sort_mixedcap_rule: Niches no longer hold the same amount: one takes two goods, another four, the rest three. The notches under a niche show how many fit and how many are taken. Check them BEFORE you move — a narrow niche fills up sooner than it looks.
lr_goods_sort_mono_example: Example: a banana, a loaf and a teddy — all warm, all alike as a blob. They differ in shape: long, wide, with ears.
lr_goods_sort_mono_rule: Here every good sits in one colour family, and colour stops helping. Usually you spot a pair with the corner of your eye — by a yellow patch; not now. You will have to look at shape: the outline, the cap, the proportions. The rules are the same; what changes is what you tell them apart by.
lr_goods_sort_movelimit_example: Example: ⇄ 12/18 — 12 of 18 moves used. The limit tightens every level.
lr_goods_sort_movelimit_rule: Each level now allows a limited number of moves — spend them wisely. Exceed the limit and the level restarts. The header counter shows used/limit.
lr_goods_sort_moving_example: Example: you lined up a cola for the second niche — after the shift that niche is the fifth. The cola and the room are still there; the address changed.
lr_goods_sort_moving_rule: Every five moves the niches move house: the contents stay, the place does not. Only niches of equal size swap, so nothing overflows. You can still see what is where; what you cannot plan ahead is the ROUTE. Play from the board in front of you, not from a plan made five moves ago.
lr_goods_sort_showcase_example: Example: you cannot see a free niche — check the map on the right: a light dot sits lower, so scroll the shelf down.
lr_goods_sort_showcase_rule: From this level the cabinet no longer fits on one screen — you can scroll it up and down. The goods do NOT get smaller: instead of shrinking, the shelf grows downwards. A map strip appears on the right: one dot per niche, light dots are free, and the frame shows which part of the shelf you are looking at.
lr_goods_sort_showcase_title: The shelf runs taller than the screen
lr_goods_sort_singlecap_example: Example: one notch under a niche. Put the cola there and the niche is taken until you take the cola back.
lr_goods_sort_singlecap_rule: Some niches have a single notch — exactly ONE good fits there. Put something in and the space is gone: only that same good can come back out, and nothing can join it. This is not a small shelf but a lock: think a move ahead about what goes in.
lr_goods_sort_strict_example: Example: a niche holds cola — only cola goes on top. Kefir will not fit there; it needs an empty niche or another kefir.
lr_goods_sort_strict_rule: On this level a good goes only into an EMPTY niche or on top of the SAME good. No more dropping anything anywhere — think a move ahead or you will block your own way.
lr_hanoi_pegs4_example: Example: the extra peg gives you two "buffers" for small discs.
lr_hanoi_pegs4_rule: There are now four pegs. More room to maneuver — but the optimal path is different, old 3-peg habits won't work. The goal stays the same: rebuild the tower on the last (rightmost) peg.
lr_hanoi_pegs5_example: Example: three "buffers" — park small discs in parallel.
lr_hanoi_pegs5_rule: Five pegs now — even more room to maneuver, but more discs too, and the optimal path changes again. The goal stays the same: the whole tower on the last (rightmost) peg.
lr_kids_sort_switches_example: Example: you sort by shape and get ✓ ✓ ✓, then a ✗: go back to colour.
lr_kids_sort_switches_rule: From now on the rule changes more than once: colour, then shape, then colour again. Each time the only sign is a ✗ where you were right a moment ago.
lr_listening_span_similar_example: You heard "casa" — and "cama" will sit right next to it in the grid. Pick what you heard, not what looks close.
lr_listening_span_similar_rule: From this level the extra words in the grid are picked to SOUND LIKE the ones you heard. They are easy to confuse, so hold not just the words but their order.
lr_listening_span_span8_example: A shorter gap means less time to repeat what you heard in your head — and that repetition is what holds the list.
lr_listening_span_span8_rule: The list stops growing here: eight is the limit of auditory span for almost everyone. What shrinks from now on is the gap between words — from 0.7 seconds down to 0.5.
lr_mahjong_hidden_example: Example: a “?” sits under a top tile — it may hide the pair you need, or a tile that locks the bottom. Decide: reveal it, or approach from another edge.
lr_mahjong_hidden_rule: On this level the faces of covered tiles are hidden — a “?” instead of the picture. You learn what lies below only by removing what is on top. You have to plan under uncertainty and revise as you go. Every third level will be like this.
lr_mahjong_layers2_example: Example: a tile under another tile, or squeezed by neighbors on both sides, cannot be tapped — free it first.
lr_mahjong_layers2_rule: Tiles now stack in 2 layers. You can only pick a FREE tile: nothing lies on it AND its left or right side is open. Dimmed tiles are blocked.
lr_mahjong_layers3_example: Example: a bottom tile becomes available once everything covering it is removed and one of its sides is open.
lr_mahjong_layers3_rule: The pyramid now has 3 layers. Same rule: a tile is free when NOTHING lies on it and its left OR right side is open. Dismantle the pyramid top-down.
lr_mahjong_layers4_example: Example: a bottom pair can become unreachable if you open the middle from the wrong side. Think two moves ahead.
lr_mahjong_layers4_rule: Four layers now, and you get one shuffle per level. The free-tile rule is unchanged — what changes is the cost of a mistake: clear from the top and the edges, or you will lock the bottom.
lr_mahjong_layers5_example: Example: two identical tiles are free, but one of them caps the last pair — take the other one.
lr_mahjong_layers5_rule: Five layers — a narrow top over a wide base. One shuffle. You can no longer take just any available pair: almost every tile you remove opens or locks something below.
lr_math_sprint_chain_rule: Two steps in one: multiply first, then add or subtract.
lr_math_sprint_div_rule: Division band (÷) — always exact, no remainder.
lr_math_sprint_equation_rule: Solve for x: work it out in your head and type it. From here on, equations mix with other topics.
lr_math_sprint_mult_rule: Multiplication band: from times tables to two-digit factors.
lr_math_sprint_root_rule: Square roots — the answer is always whole: which number squared gives this?
lr_math_sprint_square_rule: A number squared: multiply it by itself.
lr_memory_matrix_decoys_example: Four cells flashed, one of them crossed — memorise three.
lr_memory_matrix_decoys_rule: Some cells light up with a cross — these are distractors. Do not memorise them, and do not tap them: that counts as a mistake.
lr_memory_matrix_fast_example: Do not scan cell by cell, you will not make it. Look at the middle and catch the pattern with peripheral vision.
lr_memory_matrix_fast_rule: There is almost no time to look: the flash lasts less than a second. It is not the closer look that works but the wider one — centre your gaze and take the board in at once.
lr_memory_matrix_fast_title: The flash is under a second
lr_memory_matrix_grid6_example: On a big board it is easier to remember cells as a shape — "corner on the left", "diagonal" — than one by one.
lr_memory_matrix_grid6_rule: The board has grown to 6×6 and stops there. What grows from now on is the number of cells to remember, and the display gets shorter.
lr_memory_matrix_grid6_title: The grid has hit its limit
lr_memory_matrix_two_series_example: First three purple cells flashed, then three red ones — start with the purple.
lr_memory_matrix_two_series_rule: Two sets of cells now light up in different colours, one after the other. Repeat them in turn: the purple set first, then the red one.
lr_mental_rotation_cubes_example: Example: level 6 is the same task as level 1, but the shape has five cubes — one more block to hold in mind.
lr_mental_rotation_cubes_rule: From level 6 the shape has five cubes, and one more is added every five levels — up to thirteen at level 46. Within each five the rotation pattern cycles: one axis, two quarter-turns, two axes, four options, foils with one cube moved.
lr_mnemonics_method_example: Two that work: the chain — link each word to the next with an absurd image; the room — place the words around a familiar space and walk it in your mind.
lr_mnemonics_method_rule: From seven or eight items, plain repetition no longer holds the list — that is the limit, and it is about the same for everyone. Past it, only a method works.
lr_mnemonics_method_title: Repeating in your head stops working
lr_n_back_dual_example: Example (2-back): position same as 2 steps ago → "Position"; letter same as 2 steps ago → "Sound".
lr_n_back_dual_rule: Now TWO streams at once: the position on the grid and a letter (sound). Mark a position match with the "Position" button, a letter match with "Sound". You can tap both.
lr_n_back_switch_example: Example: 6-back switched to 5-back — a repeat from 6 steps ago is now a lure, not a match; a match is 5 steps back.
lr_n_back_switch_rule: Now the depth changes during the round: N and N − 1 take turns in stretches. When it switches, you'll see “Now N-back”, and N in the header shows the current depth. Compare with the step that applies right now.
lr_nut_sort_hidden_example: Example: a “?” sits under the blue nut. Screw the blue one away and it opens: a yellow nut was hiding there.
lr_nut_sort_hidden_rule: One nut on a bolt is covered by a question mark — it has a colour, but you cannot see it. It opens by itself once nothing is left above it. Such a level has no move minimum: scouting costs moves. Screw across, find out and replan — undo is free.
lr_nut_sort_movelimit_example: Example: the limit is 40 and you have used 38 — two moves left to finish screwing. Not enough means the level restarts with the same bolts.
lr_nut_sort_movelimit_rule: From this level the round has a move limit, shown at the top. It has slack: roughly a quarter of the moves above flawless play is left for changing your mind. Undo does NOT give a move back: change your mind and you have spent it. Levels with hidden nuts have no limit — scouting costs moves there.
lr_nut_sort_movelimit_title: A move limit for the nuts
lr_nut_sort_sealed_example: Example: the lock lifts once the first colour is done. So the first colour must be finished without this bolt.
lr_nut_sort_sealed_rule: One bolt is locked: nuts can neither go on nor come off until you have completed enough colours. The lock lifts by itself — it counts finished COLOURS, not moves. Until then you have to manage with the other bolts.
lr_nut_sort_short_example: Example: a bolt that holds three nuts. There are five red ones, so this bolt cannot be their home.
lr_nut_sort_short_rule: One bolt is shorter than the rest — it holds fewer nuts. It still counts as a full home: a colour completed there is finished like anywhere else. But a colour of five nuts will not fit on a bolt for four — take it elsewhere, or split it and gather it later.
lr_nut_sort_stones_example: Example: you park the blue nuts there to reach the yellow ones below. Before you finish, those blue nuts have to come back off.
lr_nut_sort_stones_rule: One bolt has a sleeve stuck at its base — it cannot be removed. You may screw nuts onto it, and that is its whole purpose: temporary storage. But it will never become a colour’s home, and the level only comes together once it is empty again.
lr_ospan_hardmath_rule: Equations now include multiplication and bigger numbers. Solve carefully — it is the distractor task; keep memorizing the letters in between.
lr_picture_pairs_quad_example: Example: 🐱🐱🐱 is not enough — you need a fourth 🐱.
lr_picture_pairs_quad_rule: Now a match is FOUR identical pictures. Open all four in a row to clear the group.
lr_picture_pairs_swap_example: Example: you remember 🐱 in the corner, and the corner lights up together with the middle — now 🐱 is in the middle.
lr_picture_pairs_swap_rule: From this level, after every mistake face-down cards swap places — one pair at a time, and the pair lights up. The higher the level, the more swaps. Watch the highlight: a card you remembered may have moved.
lr_picture_pairs_triple_example: Example: 🐱🐱 is not enough — the group clears only with a third 🐱.
lr_picture_pairs_triple_rule: From this level a match is not a pair but THREE identical pictures. Open three in a row: two of a kind is not a match yet.
lr_pizza_sort_queue_example: Example: the queue shows 2. You complete a pizza, the board leaves, and the first one from the queue takes its place at once.
lr_pizza_sort_queue_rule: Some boards wait their turn and come out by themselves — as soon as a spot frees up, that is, when you complete a whole pizza. The queue is finite and shown in the header: it is not an endless stream but a delayed part of this very level. So free up space in good time instead of piling a mix onto every board.
lr_prl_noisy_example: At this noise level a single answer tells you nothing. Hold the last three or four in mind: once losses outnumber wins, the rule has flipped.
lr_prl_noisy_rule: The good circle is no longer reliable: it used to win almost always, now noticeably less often. And the sides swap more frequently.
lr_prl_reversal_example: So two errors in a row after a long good streak is almost never bad luck — it is the rule changing. Switch. A single error means nothing: even the good circle misleads sometimes.
lr_prl_reversal_rule: One of the two circles pays off more often. Which one is unknown at first — you find out by trying. After a few correct choices in a row the sides SILENTLY swap: the good one becomes the bad one. You will get no warning.
lr_prl_reversal_title: Not a guessing game — a noticing game
lr_pseudoword_echo_longer6_example: Example: it was "nolap", now it is "viruntek". The second one only holds in pieces.
lr_pseudoword_echo_longer6_rule: It was four or five letters, now it is six or seven. A word this long no longer fits whole — you have to break it into syllables.
lr_pseudoword_echo_longer8_example: The answer options now differ by one letter in the middle — exactly where hearing fails most often.
lr_pseudoword_echo_longer8_rule: Maximum length. At this size it is not memory that decides but how precisely you heard every sound.
lr_reading_span_load_example: Do not loop the words in your head — judging the next sentence will break the loop. Tie the words into one phrase, however absurd.
lr_reading_span_load_rule: From this level the set is longer than fits in your head as a list. That is exactly what the test measures: judge the sentence and do NOT lose the words from the previous ones.
lr_reading_span_load_title: More sentences than you can hold in a row
lr_semantic_sort_four_example: The difference between "fruit" and "berry" starts to matter here.
lr_semantic_sort_four_rule: A fourth basket. General meaning is no longer enough — you need the precise feature of the word.
lr_semantic_sort_three_example: Example: it was "food or animal", now it is "fruit, vegetable or animal".
lr_semantic_sort_three_rule: Until now you chose between two baskets, now there are three. Guessing blindly got three times harder — you actually have to know the word.
lr_set_game_timelimit_example: Example: L11 — 26 s per SET, then −4 s per level (8 s minimum).
lr_set_game_timelimit_rule: You now have limited time to find a SET. Run out — penalty ✗ and a fresh board. The limit tightens every level.
lr_spatial_span_grid5_rule: The board grew to 5×5 — more cells, each one smaller. The order is still reversed.
lr_spatial_span_hold_example: The cells have finished flashing, the board stays quiet for a couple of seconds — only then you answer, from the last one back to the first.
lr_spatial_span_hold_rule: From this level a pause appears between the last flash and your input, and it grows further on. The order is still reversed, and you have to hold it in mind for longer — the grid and the pace stay the same.
lr_spatial_span_hold_title: A pause before the reverse answer
lr_stroop_noise_example: Example: they are not part of the task. Look only at the stimulus itself.
lr_stroop_noise_rule: Extra symbols appear around the stimulus. They mean nothing — the task is exactly the same, it is just harder to find what matters.
lr_stroop_switch_example: Example: the word "RED" is written in blue ink. If the line mentions INK colour, tap the blue swatch; if it mentions word MEANING, tap the red one.
lr_stroop_switch_rule: Sometimes the task changes mid-game: instead of the INK colour you answer by the word MEANING, or the other way round. The line under the word tells you which rule applies right now. Read it before every answer: the higher the level, the more often it switches.
lr_switching_task_noise_example: Example: a shape is neither a digit nor a letter — it is not judged.
lr_switching_task_noise_rule: Extra shapes appear around the digit and the letter. Judge only what the cue at the top asks for.
lr_visual_search_conj_example: Example: find the blue T. A yellow T and a blue L are decoys.
lr_visual_search_conj_rule: The target is now defined by TWO features: the right shape in the right color. Same shape in another color is NOT a target.
lr_visual_search_multi_example: Example: 🎯 1/3 — one of three targets found.
lr_visual_search_multi_rule: A round can now hold several targets — find ALL of them, the 🎯 counter shows progress.
lr_water_sort_hidden_example: Example: a “?” sits under the blue. Pour the blue away and it opens: yellow was hiding there.
lr_water_sort_hidden_rule: One layer in a tube is covered by a question mark — there is a colour there, but you cannot see it. It opens by itself once nothing remains above it. Such a level has no move minimum: scouting costs moves, and the count is not judged by them. Pour, find out, replan — undo is free.
lr_water_sort_movelimit_example: Example: the limit is 40 and you have spent 38 — two moves left to finish. Not enough means the level restarts with the same board.
lr_water_sort_movelimit_rule: From this level the round has a move limit — it is shown at the top. It is not «as many as it takes»: it leaves roughly a quarter of the moves above flawless play for changing your mind. Undo does NOT give a move back: you changed your mind, you spent it. On hidden-layer levels there is no limit — scouting costs moves and there is nothing to measure them against.
lr_water_sort_sealed_example: Example: the lock lifts once the first colour is done. So the first colour must be finished without this vessel.
lr_water_sort_sealed_rule: One vessel is locked: it neither takes nor gives until you have completed enough colours. The lock lifts by itself — it counts finished COLOURS, not moves. Until then you have to manage with the rest.
lr_water_sort_short_example: Example: a vessel holding three. Red has five portions, so this vessel cannot be its home.
lr_water_sort_short_rule: One vessel is lower than the rest — it holds fewer portions. It still counts as a full home: a colour completed there is finished like anywhere else. But a colour of five portions will not fit into a vessel of four — take it elsewhere, or split it and gather it later.
lr_water_sort_stones_example: Example: you park blue there to reach the yellow underneath. Before you finish, that blue has to come back out.
lr_water_sort_stones_rule: One vessel has stones on its floor — they cannot be moved. You may pour into it, and that is exactly its purpose: temporary storage. But it will never become a colour’s home, and the level only comes together once it is empty again.
lr_word_pairs_faster_example: Saying them out loud stops fitting around level 8 — link the pair with an image instead, it is faster.
lr_word_pairs_faster_rule: Every level adds pairs and takes away seconds. A pair is shown for 7 seconds at level 1, about 4 by level 10, then 2.5.
lr_word_pairs_fifteen_example: At this size you cannot hold pairs separately: chain them so each one pulls the next.
lr_word_pairs_fifteen_rule: The list has hit its ceiling — fifteen pairs. From here only the pace keeps rising.
lspanConfigDesc: Listen to words in your target language and recall them in order. Ear training + working memory.
lspanLvlAuto: Lv {n} — {s} words by ear, grows with results (more words → faster pace)
lspanMemorizeHint: Memorize the words and their order — the screen will not show them
lspanRecallHint: Tap the words you heard IN THE SAME ORDER ({i} of {n})
mahjongIntroDesc: Classic mahjong solitaire. Tiles are stacked in a pyramid. A tile is FREE when nothing covers it from above AND its left OR right side is open. Tap two free tiles with the same symbol — the pair disappears. Blocked tiles are dimmed and do not respond. Goal — clear EVERY tile. Stuck? The "Shuffle" button reshuffles the remaining tiles. Levels ramp up: more tiles and more layers.
mahjongNoPairs: No pairs available — the board is stuck. Shuffle or undo a move.
mahjongStuckRestart: No pairs left, nothing to shuffle or undo. This level has to be restarted.
mahjongStuckShuffle: No pairs available — the board is stuck. Shuffle.
mahjongStuckUndo: No pairs available — the board is stuck. Undo a move.
mathSliderDesc: Estimate the result and place a marker on the number line
mathSliderIntroDesc: Estimate the value of the expression and place a marker on the number line. Exact calculation is not the point — landing in the right region of the scale is. Builds number sense and approximation, and the expression family itself changes with the levels: addition, subtraction, multiplication, decimals, percentages, discounts, proportions.
mathSprintDesc: Solve as many problems as possible in time
mathSprintIntroDesc: Type the answer on the keys below — a correct one counts at once. Solve arithmetic problems against the clock. Consecutive correct answers grow a streak bonus. Builds mental arithmetic and processing speed.
memoryMatrixIntroDesc: Cells flash briefly — then tap the same ones. Trains visuospatial memory.
memoryPalaceDesc: Place items along a route and recall them forward and in reverse
memoryPalaceIntroDesc: Trains the method of loci: study a route, tie each item to a place, and recall them by location in both directions.
mentalRotationDesc: Find the rotated copy of a shape
mentalRotationIntroDesc: The reference is at the top, the answer options below. In the main task, “Rotation”, pick the same shape, just turned: the other options are its mirror image or a different shape. As you level up, new tasks join in: “Projection”, “Cube net”, “Viewpoint”, “Same figure”, “Assembly”, “Memory”, “Three views”, “Slice”, “Missing piece” and “Cross-section”; each one’s question is written above the reference. Trains spatial reasoning and mental rotation. Before a round you can pick one task kind and practise just that.
mnemFreeTrainingNote: Any number of items. Your level does not change.
mnemonicsGroupDesc: Tie the new to what you already know
mnemonicsGroupFootnote: The shared trick: the new is remembered not on its own but hooked to the known — a place, a face, a word, an image.
mnemonicsGroupIntroDesc:
Four techniques of one trick: the new gets hooked to the known. Mnemonics turn a list into images; the Memory Palace lays them along a familiar route; Faces and Names ties a name to a feature; Word Pairs link two words so one pulls the other.

Memory holds isolated things badly and connected things well. So you remember not by effort but by hook: a place, a face, a word, an image. All four train exactly that.
mnemonicsIntroDesc: Memorize a sequence of words or numbers in the correct order. Develops working memory — the ability to hold information in mind.
monsterMissingDesc: Remember every monster while they are on the table. Then one is removed — pick it from the options. The options look like the missing one: you can tell them apart only if you remembered its colour, body and eyes. Three tries per level, two must be right.
monsterTraitsDesc: Mark every monster with the named trait — colour, body shape or number of eyes — and press Check. Only the exact set counts: none missed, none extra.
msg_backup_copied_full: The full backup is copied to the clipboard. Paste it into notes or a file and keep it safe. To restore — copy that text and tap “Restore from backup”.
msg_paste_backup_json: Copy the backup text (JSON) to the clipboard, then tap “Restore from backup” again.
msg_reset_unlocks_confirm: All previously entered codes will be forgotten. To restore the profiles you will need to enter the codes again.
nBackDesc: Does flash position match one from N steps back?
nBackDualHint: Tap Position if the position repeats {n} back. Tap Sound if the letter repeats {n} back. You can tap both
nBackHint: Compare current flash with one N steps ago — if same position → MATCH
nBackIntroDesc:
🧠 Most effective working memory trainer (Jaeggi et al., 2008 — the only paradigm with proven IQ transfer effect).

📋 HOW TO PLAY:
• Cells flash on the grid one at a time
• Remember the position N steps ago
• When current flash MATCHES the position from N steps back → press MATCH
• If it doesn't match — don't press, wait for next

🎯 EXAMPLE for N=2 (track positions 2 steps back):
Step 1: flash top-left   → wait
Step 2: flash right      → wait
Step 3: flash bottom-left → COMPARE with step 1 (top-left). Doesn't match → don't press
Step 4: flash right      → COMPARE with step 2 (right). MATCH! → press ✓

💡 STRATEGY for beginners:
• Start with N=1 (track just the previous flash) until rhythm clicks
• Then N=2, then N=3. Above N=4 is elite-level
• Don't try to "remember all steps" — your brain runs a sliding window automatically
• 15-20 min/day for 3-4 weeks → noticeable WM gains
navigatorDesc: Remember routes, turn sequences, and the direction back to the start
navigatorIntroDesc: First study the route on the map, then repeat it with the direction buttons below the board — keys or a swipe across the board work too. In other modes, recall the turns in order or point to where the start is. Trains spatial memory.
noMovesUndo: No moves left — undo a move
numberBondsDesc: Find numbers that sum to target
numberBondsIntroDesc: The target number is at the top. Tap chips to make exactly that sum: two or three are enough at first, more later on. Tapped a wrong one — tap it again to remove it; “Reset” clears everything. Once the sum is right, press “Check”. Each puzzle is timed — the counter runs at the top: running out or getting the sum wrong counts as an error, and two are allowed per level. Trains mental arithmetic and combination search.
numberRunDesc: Steer a number down the road and decide on the move what to pick up: blue adds, red subtracts.
numberRunIntroDesc: You steer one number down the road and decide on the move what to pick up. A blue number adds what is written on it, a red one subtracts. Your number takes what its middle runs over, not what its edges brush: to take several numbers from one row, slide your number sideways right through them. Follow a snake of blues with your finger and swerve around the reds beside it. A pole splits the road in two: pick your side before it by the sum of that stack — you cannot cross the pole. Of a row of walls across the road you drive through one, and its action applies to your number: take the smaller minus, or compare ×2 with the plus. The green pad throws you across a gap — miss it and you fall — and carries you over a big red. Twelve stages run back to back, with no stops and no reset of your number; at the finish your number smashes through as many walls as it can. In level mode the road brings Counting hub tasks: a problem over three arches — drive into the arch with the right answer; amber numbers — collect exactly the number on the sign. Every third level is held by a guardian: reach the finish with at least its number. A number sequence on the sign — drive into the arch with its next term; a number line across the road — pass where the value of the expression lies. Remember the symbols above the road in order: a stretch later, pick them in the same order.
numberRunLevelsHint: A level lasts 90 seconds. Counting hub tasks join one at a time: problems over arches from level 4, “collect exactly N” from 7, number sequences from 10, the number line from 13, symbol memory from 16. Every third level has a guardian.
numberRunMarathonHint: Free: the full run without levels — 12 stages back to back, 8:24.
numberRunRecall: Pick the symbols in the same order
numberRunRule: Steer your number down the road: blue adds, red subtracts. At a pole, pick the side by the sum of its stack; at walls, take the smaller minus. The green ramp throws you over a gap and over a big red. At the finish your number smashes through as many walls as it can.
nutSortDesc: Sort nuts onto bolts: one colour per bolt
nutSortIntroDesc: Tap a bolt to lift its top run of one colour, tap another to screw them on. You may only add onto the same colour or onto an empty bolt, and only while there is room. The level is done when every bolt is empty or holds one colour. Think ahead about where the colour in your way will go: there are only two free bolts.
objectTrackerDesc: Track marked objects in a moving group and identify them after motion stops
objectTrackerIntroDesc: Trains dynamic attention: memorize the targets, keep track of them during motion, and select them after they stop.
oneLineDesc: Draw one continuous line across every edge without using any edge twice
oneLineIntroDesc: Tap the vertices one after another — the line runs along the edge between them. Draw one continuous line across every edge of the graph exactly once. You may revisit vertices, but an edge you have already used is spent. A place where two lines cross on screen is not a vertex — you cannot turn there. Trains route planning: nearly every move is legal on its own, yet many lead to a dead end from which the remaining edges cannot be collected. Levels grow the graph rather than the speed: more vertices, triangle branches, more tangled layouts, and the hint that marks a legal start disappears after level three.
ospanIntroDesc: Answer “Correct” or “Incorrect” to each equation and remember the letter; at the end type the letters in order and press “Check”. Alternate: equation "is it correct?" → remember a letter → equation → letter → ... After N iterations type the letters IN ORDER. Dual load: arithmetic + storage. Operation Span — the gold standard for working memory under load.
ospanRecallPrompt: Name the letters in order — there are {n}
ospanResultFail: {n} slips — a level counts only with a perfect recall
ospanResultWin: Level cleared: all {n} letters in order
outOfLivesHint: Mistakes: {n} of {n}. Play again — fresh board.
pairsDuelHint: Take turns with a bot. Find a pair — go again. You see the bot's cards too.
pairsKidsHint: Open two cards at a time and find the pairs. Fewer moves — more stars. No clock.
pairsModeLevelsHint: Levels ramp: win → next, harder. Score accumulates.
passCorrect80Window: To pass: ≥80% correct answers (missing the window counts as an error)
patternClassMixed: Any hard series — numbers grow with the level
patternIntroDesc: Tap the number below that continues the sequence. You see 4 numbers — they follow a hidden rule (arithmetic, doubling, squares, Fibonacci, etc.). Find the next number. Trains abstract thinking, pattern detection and mathematical intuition.
patternRuleLinear: Each term is the previous × {a}, then {b}
pauseDesc: Plus face, posture, relaxation and mobility — a short body pause with no scoring
pauseIntroDesc: Choose the setting, the minutes and what to practise — the app guides you step by step. Nothing here is measured or scored: this is rest, not a test.
phPairsConfigDesc: Listen to the word and pick what you heard — ship or sheep? Trains phonemic hearing.
phPairsLvlAuto: Lv {n} — grows with results: more trials → all pairs → no visual hints
phPairsPickHint: What did you hear? Pick the word.
phonemePairsDesc: Hear the difference: ship or sheep?
phonemePairsIntroDesc:
Two words sound nearly identical and differ by a single sound: ship or sheep, bad or bed. You listen and pick which one was said.

Your native language mutes foreign sounds: the ones it lacks get bent into familiar shapes until you stop hearing the difference at all. This brings that distinction back — and both understanding fast speech and your own pronunciation start there.
phonemicDesc: Name max words on a letter in 60s
phonemicHint: Words starting with "{L}". Press Enter after each
phonemicIntroDesc: COWAT (Controlled Oral Word Association Test) — classic verbal fluency test. In 60s name max words starting with a given letter. No proper names, no repetitions. Biomarkers: word_count, mean_inter_word_sec (time between words — higher = harder lexical access), first_half vs second_half (endurance). Direct measure of lexical access under time pressure — critical for public speaking and negotiations.
phonemicRules: Rules: common nouns only, length ≥ 2, no repetitions
picturePairsHint: Flip two cards at a time and remember what is where
picturePairsIntroDesc: Flip two cards at a time and find matching pairs. Fewer moves = higher score. Trains visual memory and matching.
pizzaSortDesc: Gather a circle of six matching slices
pizzaSortIntroDesc: Gather a circle of six matching pizza slices. A slice only goes onto a matching one or onto an empty board. Complete the circle and the board leaves, freeing the spot.
playlistsNowFactory: Now: factory playlists from the build
playlistsPasteHint: Copy the playlist file to the clipboard and try again
posnerDesc: React to target; cue may mislead
posnerHint: Where did target appear? Don't trust cue blindly
posnerIntroDesc: A dot in the centre — keep your eyes on it. A cue flashes to one side: usually it is right, sometimes it misleads you, sometimes it points nowhere. Then the target appears — press the side it showed up on. When the cue misled you, the answer comes out noticeably slower. That is what the game measures: how much time a true cue saves and a false one costs. The Posner cueing task, 1980.
posnerLvlParams: {n} trials · cue valid ~{p}% · {w} s response window
prlDesc: One of 2 colors pays +10. When rule reverses — switch
prlHint: Pick a circle. Rule may change — watch feedback
prlIntroDesc: Two circles. One pays more often, the other is mostly empty — which is which is not stated, you work it out as you go. No guessing is needed: watch what pays and stay with it. The catch is that the circles quietly swap round now and then, and the good one becomes the bad one. There is no warning: the only sign is that a choice that was working suddenly stops. Two or three misses in a row after a good run mean it is time to try the other circle. The game is not watching your luck but how quickly you notice the change, and whether you keep stubbornly to the old choice. The classic reversal-learning task, Cools 2002.
prlLvlParams: {n} trials · reward {p}% · reversal every {a}-{b} correct in a row
prlNote: Key rule: after several correct in a row, rules swap. Don't persist with old choice.
prlPass: To pass: ≥{p}% correct choices after reversals

profileDesc_execs: Decisions under pressure · risk · WM · flexibility
profileDesc_free: 9 trainers · a curated set to start with
profileDesc_kids: Memory · counting · reaction · no complex abstractions
profileDesc_polyglot: For languages: verbal memory · associations · fluency · scripts
profileDesc_students: Focus · memory · speed · SAT / GMAT / GRE / IELTS
profileDesc_vasilyeva: Visual field · eye speed · text retention
profileDesc_women: Addictive casual games for micro-breaks: pairs, spot-the-difference, hidden object, sudoku
proofPass: To pass: find ≥{p}% of targets before time runs out (false taps and misses cost stars)
proofreadingIntroDesc:
Two tasks under one card, switched at the top.
"Letters" is the proofreading task: find every target symbol in a dense grid and miss none. The further you go, the bigger the grid and the less time per cell.
"Words" is a word-snake: words hide in the grid along a bending path and you trace them.
What the two share is holding attention on monotonous material. The game watches what you miss, not how fast you go.
pseudowordEchoDesc: Hear a made-up word — pick its spelling
pseudowordEchoIntroDesc:
You hear an invented word — one that exists in no language. Your task is to pick how it is spelled.

Why invented: a real word is recognised whole, from memory, and never has to be broken into sounds. An invented one closes that shortcut — you must hold the sound in your head and take it apart. That is a clean measure of phonological memory, the thing new foreign vocabulary rests on.
