puzzleErrUnknownMode: the engine does not know the mode {mode}
puzzlesBlackBoxDesc: Find the hidden balls from where each beam leaves the box
puzzlesBlackBoxIntroDesc: Balls are hidden inside a closed box and you must find them without looking in. Tapping an arrow on the edge fires a beam: it travels straight, deflects when it passes beside a ball, and is absorbed when it hits one. From where the beam comes out, returns, or fails to appear at all, the positions follow with certainty. Tapping a cell inside places a guess “a ball is here”, a long press marks the cell as empty so you don’t lose track. Place every ball and the box opens to show where they really were.
puzzlesBridgesDesc: Join the islands: the number counts bridges, a double counts two. Drag island to island. Bridges never cross; all must connect.
puzzlesCubeDesc: Steer with the arrows: the solid rolls over an edge and picks up markers with its faces
puzzlesCubeIntroDesc: Goal: collect every marker on the faces of the solid. Steer with the arrows: it tips over an edge and picks a marker up with whichever face lands on it. Rolling back over a square puts the marker down again, so the order of your route decides everything.
puzzlesDominosaDesc: Rebuild how a full set of dominoes lies on the grid. Tap the line between two numbers to join them; the second action marks that no domino is there
puzzlesDominosaIntroDesc: A full set of dominoes once lay on the board: every pair of numbers from 0 up to the largest appears exactly once. The dominoes were removed and only the numbers stayed — work out where each one lay. Tap the line between two neighbouring numbers to lay a domino there; tap again to remove it. The “No domino” button or a long press draws a bar meaning “these two numbers are not one domino”. The number buttons below the board highlight every cell with that number, up to two numbers at once. Example: there is only one 0-0 domino in the set — if two zeros sit side by side in just one place, it lies there.
puzzlesFifteenDesc: Tap a tile next to the gap, or use the arrows — restore the order
puzzlesFifteenIntroDesc: Goal: put the numbers in order with the gap at the end. Tap a tile NEXT TO the gap and it slides in; tapping anything else does nothing. The arrows are easier — they cannot miss a tile.
puzzlesFillingDesc: Each cell holds the size of its own connected region. Tap a cell, then a digit below
puzzlesFlipDesc: Tap cells: each tap flips it and its neighbours. Turn the whole board off
puzzlesFlipIntroDesc: Goal: turn the whole board off. Tap cells: each tap flips the cell and its neighbours in a cross. Order does not matter, the choice does — tapping the same cell twice is the same as not tapping it.
puzzlesFloodDesc: Flood the whole board with a single colour inside the move limit. Tap a square of the colour you want.
puzzlesGalaxiesDesc: Cut the grid into regions, each symmetric about its one dot. Tap a line for a wall; a correct region changes colour
puzzlesGalaxiesIntroDesc: Cut the board with walls into regions. Each region holds exactly one dot and is symmetric around it: turn it half a turn about the dot and it lands on itself. A dot sits in the middle of a cell, on the wall between two cells, or on a corner. Every cell belongs to some region, and there are no extra walls inside a region. Example: around a dot on the wall between two cells, a region of just those two cells works. A correct region changes colour at once — white for a white dot, dark for a black dot. A grey cell is not yet in a correct region, and while any grey remains the puzzle is not solved. Tap the line between cells to place or remove a wall. The “Mark” button draws reminder arrows for yourself; you don't need them to solve.
puzzlesGuessDesc: Deduce the hidden colour code from hit-and-place clues
puzzlesGuessIntroDesc: A row of colours is hidden and you have a limited number of tries to name it. Build your row and submit; the answer comes back as markers: how many colours sit in the RIGHT place, and how many are in the code but placed elsewhere. Which marker belongs to which peg is never revealed, so every try is a deduction from the previous ones rather than a sweep. Tap a slot to set a colour, long press to clear it, then confirm the row with the button below the board.
puzzlesInertiaDesc: Slide with the arrows until you hit something: gather the gems, dodge the mines. Move with the arrows, diagonals too.
puzzlesKeenDesc: In each cage, the arithmetic must equal the number in its corner. Tap a cell, then a digit below; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesLightUpDesc: Light the whole grid with lamps. Tap to place a lamp; the second action marks a cell as “no lamp”
puzzlesLightUpIntroDesc: Light up every white cell. A lamp lights its own cell and shines in straight lines in all four directions until a black cell. No two lamps may shine on each other. A number on a black cell says how many lamps sit right next to it — above, below, left and right; a black cell without a number can have any number of lamps beside it. Example: 0 means no lamp beside it, 4 means lamps on all four sides. Tap to place or remove a lamp; the “No lamp” button or a long press marks “no lamp here”. Lit cells turn yellow and mistakes turn red: it is solved when everything is yellow and nothing is red.
puzzlesLoopyDesc: Build one closed loop guided by the numbers. Tap between two dots to draw a line.
puzzlesMagnetsDesc: Edge numbers: top and left count the “+” in that line, bottom and right the “−”. Tap for a magnet; “Empty” lays blank dominoes — they count too
puzzlesMagnetsIntroDesc: The board is split into dominoes — you only see their outlines. Each domino is either a magnet with a “+” end and a “−” end, or blank. The numbers around the board count poles in their line: top and left say how many “+”, bottom and right how many “−”; a line with no number is free. Equal poles never touch side by side; blank halves can sit anywhere. Example: a row with 2 on the left and 1 on the right holds two “+” and one “−”, and all its other cells are blank. Tap a domino to lay a magnet with “+” on that half; tap again to flip it, a third time to clear it. The “Empty” button below the board, or a long press, lays a blank domino. It is solved only when every domino is decided — blank ones must be placed too.
puzzlesMapDesc: Colour the regions so that neighbours differ. Drag from a coloured region to an empty one to carry the colour; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesMapIntroDesc: Colour every region of the map with one of four colours so that neighbours sharing a border get different colours; touching only at a corner doesn't count. Regions coloured from the start can't be changed — that's where you pick colours up. Drag from a coloured region into an empty one to carry the colour over; dragging from an empty region clears a colour. With the “Pencil” button the colour goes on as hatching — a note meaning “might be this colour”, and one region can hold several. Example: a region whose three neighbours already use three different colours can only take the fourth.
puzzlesMinesDesc: The numbers say how many mines are adjacent; the board is solvable without guessing. Tap to open a cell; the second action flags a mine
puzzlesMinesIntroDesc: Mines hide under the closed cells — open every cell that has no mine. A number in an open cell says how many mines are among its eight neighbours, corners included. An open cell with no number means “no mines around”, and its neighbours open by themselves. Example: an open 1 with only one closed neighbour left — the mine is there. Tap to open a cell. The “Flag” button or a long press puts a flag for “mine here”, and a flagged cell can't be opened by accident. Tapping a number that already has that many flags around it opens the rest of its neighbours. The board is always solvable without guessing; flags are not required to win.
puzzlesMosaicDesc: A number counts the black cells in the 3×3 square around it, itself included. Tap for black, “Empty” for white; it counts once all are decided
puzzlesMosaicIntroDesc: Every cell must end up black or white. A number says how many black cells are in the 3×3 square centred on that cell, the cell itself included. At the edge the square is smaller: 4 cells in a corner, 6 along a side. Example: 9 means all nine are black, 0 means all white, a 4 in a corner means all four are black. Tap a cell to make it black; further taps make it white and then empty again. The “Empty” button or a long press starts with white. It is solved only when every cell around every number is decided — whites must be marked too.
puzzlesNetDesc: Tap a piece to turn it. Switch on “Turn back” to turn it the other way. Join the whole network
puzzlesNetIntroDesc: Goal: connect every pipe to the source with no open ends. Tap a piece to turn it a quarter. Need the other way? Switch on “Turn back” below the board: while it is lit, a tap turns the piece back.
puzzlesNetslideDesc: Tap an arrow at the edge and the whole row slides around. Pieces never turn, they only travel
puzzlesNetslideIntroDesc: The same network, but pieces never turn. Tap an arrow at the edge and the whole row or column wraps around — what leaves one side comes back on the other. One slide moves a lot at once, so plan the move first.
puzzlesPalisadeDesc: Cut the grid into regions of one size; a number says how many of the cell's sides are borders, the board edge included. Tap a line for a border
puzzlesPalisadeIntroDesc: Cut the board with borders into regions that all have the same size. The size depends on the board: on 5×5 each region has 5 cells, on 8×6 — 6, on 10×8 — 8, on 15×12 — 10. A number in a cell says how many of its four sides are borders; the edge of the board counts as a border too. Example: a corner cell with 2 — two of its sides are already the board edge, so it has no borders towards its neighbours and both belong to its region. A 0 means the cell sits inside its region on all four sides. Tap the line between two cells to place a border, tap again to remove it; the “Mark” button or a long press marks “no border here”. Solved when every region has the right size, every number fits, and there are no extra borders inside regions.
puzzlesPatternDesc: Row and column numbers are the lengths of black runs, in order. Tap for black, “Cross” for white; it counts once every cell is decided
puzzlesPatternIntroDesc: Every cell must end up black or white. The numbers left of a row are the lengths of its black runs, in order from left to right; the numbers above a column go from top to bottom. Runs are separated by at least one white cell. Example: a row marked “3 1” has three blacks in a row, then at least one white, then one black; a row marked “0” is all white. Tap to make a cell black; drag along a row or column to fill a run. The “Cross” button or a long press makes a cell white. It is solved only when every cell is decided: no grey left, whites marked too.
puzzlesPearlDesc: A closed loop: white circles need a straight, black ones a turn. Tap between cells to draw a line.
puzzlesPegsDesc: Jump a peg over its neighbour until a single peg is left. Drag a peg over its neighbour into the empty hole.
puzzlesRangeDesc: A number says how many cells are visible from it along its row and column. Tap to black out a cell; the second action puts a dot for “empty”
puzzlesRangeIntroDesc: Paint some cells black. A number says how many white cells can be seen from that cell in straight lines up, down, left and right until a black cell or the board edge, the cell itself included. A numbered cell is always white. Black cells never touch side by side, and all white cells join up into one area. Example: a 2 in a corner sees itself and exactly one more cell — so on one side the next cell is black, and on the other side there is one white and then a black. Tap to paint a cell black; the “Dot” button or a long press puts a dot for “surely white”. Dots are not required to solve.
puzzlesRectanglesDesc: Cut the grid into rectangles; the number inside is its area. Drag from corner to corner to draw a rectangle — a single tap takes one cell
puzzlesRectanglesIntroDesc: Cut the board into rectangles. Each rectangle contains exactly one number, and that number is its area — how many cells it covers; a square counts as a rectangle. Example: a 6 can be a 1×6 strip or a 2×3 block, standing or lying — pick the one that doesn't cover another number. Drag from corner to corner to draw a frame; a single tap takes one cell. With the “Erase” button, a drag wipes the lines inside without touching the frame. A correct rectangle gets shaded; the puzzle is solved when the whole board is shaded.
puzzlesSameGameDesc: Clear groups of one colour: the bigger the group, the bigger the score. Tap a group, then tap again to clear it.
puzzlesSignpostDesc: Link the numbers in order, each step along an arrow. Drag from one cell to the next.
puzzlesSinglesDesc: The numbers are already there: cross out repeats without splitting the grid. Tap a cell to cross it out; the second action circles one to keep
puzzlesSixteenDesc: Tap an arrow at the edge: that row or column wraps around. Put the numbers in order
puzzlesSixteenIntroDesc: Goal: put the numbers in order. Tap an arrow at the edge: the row or column wraps around, and what leaves one side returns on the other. Unlike the fifteen puzzle, a move shifts a whole line, not one tile.
puzzlesSlantDesc: Draw a diagonal in every cell and close no loop
puzzlesSlantIntroDesc: Draw exactly one diagonal in every cell — either “/” or “”. The numbers sit on grid corners and say how many diagonal ends meet AT THAT corner: 0 means none, 4 means all four. The key restriction: the lines must never form a closed loop, however large. A short tap flips the slash, a long press flips it the other way.
puzzlesSlideDesc: Drag a block into the free space — get the main block out
puzzlesSlideIntroDesc: Goal: get the main block out. Drag a block with your finger into the free space; it only travels straight and only while there is room. Moves are unlimited but counted — think before you push.
puzzlesSokobanDesc: Walk with the arrows and push barrels onto the marks. A cornered barrel is stuck for good
puzzlesSokobanIntroDesc: Goal: push every barrel onto a mark. Walk with the arrows; a barrel can only be PUSHED ahead of you, never pulled. A barrel forced into a corner is stuck for good — then it is undo or restart.
puzzlesSoloDesc: Digits 1–9 once per row, column and block. Tap a cell, then a digit below; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesTentsDesc: Put a tent by each tree, matching the counts on the edges. Tap for a tent; the second action marks grass
puzzlesTentsIntroDesc: Every tree needs its own tent right next to it — above, below, left or right — and there are exactly as many tents as trees. Tents never touch each other, not even diagonally. The numbers at the edge say how many tents are in that row or column. Example: a row marked 0 has no tents, so you can cover all of it with grass. Tap an empty cell to pitch a tent; the “Grass” button or a long press marks “no tent here”; tapping a filled cell clears it. Grass is not required to solve.
puzzlesTowersDesc: A number outside says how many towers are visible from there. Tap a cell, then a digit below; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesTracksDesc: Complete the track edge to edge, matching row and column counts. Drag square to square: the path sets the shape, nothing needs rotating.
puzzlesTwiddleDesc: Tap inside a square of cells and it turns as one block. Put the numbers back in order
puzzlesTwiddleIntroDesc: Goal: put the numbers in order, left to right and top to bottom. Tap inside a square of cells and it turns as one block with everything inside it. Every turn both fixes and breaks — work from a corner.
puzzlesUndeadDesc: Ghosts, vampires and zombies to match the counts in the mirrors. Tap a cell, then a monster below; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesUnequalDesc: Greater-than signs between cells fix the order. Tap a cell, then a digit below; the second action leaves a pencil mark
puzzlesUnrulyDesc: Equal black and white cells, never three of a kind in a row
puzzlesUnrulyIntroDesc: Fill the grid with black and white cells under three rules: every row and every column holds as many black cells as white; no three of a kind ever sit in a row, across or down; and no two rows or columns are identical. The cells you start with are fixed. A short tap cycles empty → black → white, a long press cycles the other way.
puzzlesUnrulyRule: Every row and column holds as many circles as dots. Three of a kind in a row never happens. Tap a cell to cycle: empty → ○ → ●
puzzlesUntangleDesc: Drag a node with your finger and pull them apart until no two lines cross
puzzlesUntangleIntroDesc: Goal: pull the nodes apart until no two lines cross. Drag a node with your finger and the lines follow it. A solution always exists, and it is usually easier to start from the node with the most lines.
pwEchoConfigDesc: Listen to a made-up word and pick its correct spelling. Trains the phonological loop — the key to vocabulary growth.
pwEchoLvlAuto: Lv {n} — grows with results (longer words → more rounds)
pwEchoPickSpelling: Pick the spelling of what you heard
pwEchoUnsupportedNote: 中文 and हिन्दी are not supported yet: sound-alike spelling options can’t be built fairly for those scripts.
qcIntro: The dots flash for an instant — say how many there were
quickCountIntroDesc: When the dots disappear, tap the button with their number below. Dots flash briefly — estimate how many without counting one by one. Trains numerosity perception (subitizing) — a skill distinct from arithmetic, the instant sense of quantity.
rbBotBust: The bot rolled a one — its unbanked progress is lost
rbBust: A one! Unbanked progress is lost
readingSpanDesc: Judge each sentence’s meaning and remember its last word
readingSpanIntroDesc: Read sentences one at a time. For each: judge whether it makes sense (✓ or ✗) AND remember the last word. After N sentences, type all the last words in order. This is the classic Daneman-Carpenter Reading Working Memory test.
recallHint: Type the last words separated by spaces in the correct order
relaxationGroupDesc: Breathing, eyes, a pause — a short rest for the mind
relaxationGroupFootnote: Nothing is measured or scored here: this is a break between workouts, not a test.
relaxationGroupIntroDesc:
Three short breaks: Breathing paces your inhale and exhale, Eyes & breathing alternates the two, Eye Gymnastics rests your eyes after the screen.

Nothing is measured here. Attention and working memory recover during pauses — after a short break the next game goes more smoothly.
rhythmPitchDesc: Echo rhythms and remember pitch sequences — by ear, no microphone
rhythmPitchIntroDesc: A short calibration comes first: four pulses let the game learn your device latency and volume. Then levels alternate: Rhythm Echo asks you to repeat the beat pattern you heard at the same timing, Pitch Path asks whether the second tone was higher or lower and later to rebuild a sequence of low, mid and high tones. There are no words at all, so language does not change the difficulty. Trains auditory working memory and a sense of timing. Sound is required: headphones or a speaker.
rmetIntroDesc: An exercise INSPIRED BY the eyes-based emotion recognition paradigm (Baron-Cohen, 2001) — it is not that test. The original uses photographs of eyes and 36 items; this one uses its own material and 18. So the original norms do NOT carry over here and you should not compare yourself against them. You see an expression and a short context, and pick one emotion out of four. The measure is accuracy. Useful wherever you must read another person’s state: negotiation, public speaking.
rollAndBankDesc: Roll the die and move forward. Roll again or bank your progress. A one burns everything unbanked and the turn passes to the bot. First to the finish wins.
rspanLvlAuto: Lv {n} — grows with results: more sentences per set
samuraiDesc: Five overlapping 9×9 grids sharing corner blocks; standard sudoku in each.
samuraiTitleIntroDesc:
Five 9×9 grids locked together at the corners: every corner block belongs to two grids at once. Ordinary sudoku rules apply within each grid separately.

All the difficulty lives in the shared blocks. A digit placed in a corner changes the picture in two grids at once, so solving them one after another does not work — you have to hold both in your head.
scholarsFlowHint: No breaks, no levels: positions keep coming until time runs out
scholarsMateDesc: A memorised pattern against the clock: what is measured is not whether you can, but how fast you see it. It starts with the scholar’s mate, then neighbouring ones arrive — queen with a knight, bishop mate, smothered mate, fool’s mate. Time per position drops from 20 seconds to 4.
scholarsMateIntroDesc: One and the same pattern: queen and bishop strike f7 — f2 for Black. Tap a piece, then a square; one move, and the bar on top is your time. Higher up the ladder there is less time and the positions come from real games; at the end come mates with a sacrifice: give up a piece first, then mate. Stars are for SPEED, not for how many you solved — you know the pattern already.
schulteIntroDesc:
Tap the symbols in order — the one to find now is shown in the bar at the top. Find symbols in order as fast as possible. 5 modifications for different challenge levels:

• 🔢 Numbers 1→25 (classic, easiest)
• 🔢 Numbers 25→1 (backward — harder)
• 🔤 Letters A→Z (same principle, alphabet)
• 🔤 Letters Z→A (backward alphabet — harder)
• 🔀 1-A-2-B-3-C (Schulte-Gorbov: switching between two sequences in parallel)

Color mode adds visual noise for extra challenge. Expands peripheral vision, speeds up information scanning, and trains sustained attention.
schulteResultFail: {errors} errors — more than {max}, level not counted
schulteRuleLetBack: Find the letters in reverse order
schulteRuleLetCenter: Find the letters from the center outward
schulteRuleMixBack: Find a number, then a letter, in turn, in reverse order
schulteRuleMixCenter: Find a number, then a letter, in turn, from the center outward
schulteRuleMixFwd: Find a number, then a letter, in turn, in order
schulteRuleNumBack: Find the numbers in reverse order
schulteRuleNumCenter: Find the numbers from the center outward
schulteSurpriseStart: Where to start — we’ll tell you once the grid is shown
sdkBoardFailed: The board could not be built
sdkGameFailed: The game could not be prepared
sdmtIntroDesc: A table maps 9 symbols ↔ 9 digits (random per game). A symbol appears — press the matching digit. Make as many correct answers as possible in the time limit. A sensitive measure of processing speed.
searchGroupDesc: Find the one among the many
searchGroupFootnote: What they share: you know what you are looking for; the difficulty is everything similar lying next to it.
searchGroupIntroDesc:
Finding the one among the many — one skill in six guises. Visual search and the proofreading test hunt a given symbol among distractors; Spot the Difference compares two pictures; mahjong looks for a pair among free tiles; Schulte tables drive the gaze across a grid; quick count asks for a quantity without counting.

The proofreading test belongs here: crossing out letters is the same search, with the target set by a symbol rather than a shape.
searchRunnerDesc: The section’s drills on the road. Above the road is the station’s question: what comes next in order, which shape you need, or which mark you tracked. Drive into the arch with the answer — tap the left or right half of the road. The level counts when you find at least 70% of the stations.
semanticSortDesc: Which category does the word belong to?
semanticSortIntroDesc: A word in the target language — assign it to the right category (food? animal? action?). Categorising without translating = direct access to L2 meaning, bypassing your native language. That is how words stick for good: not “perro = dog”, but perro → 🐾.
setGameIntroDesc: Tap the three cards that form a SET. Each card has 4 attributes: color, shape, shading, count. Find a triple where every attribute is either identical across all three or all different. Trains visual logic.
simonDesc: Color tells which button; position distracts
simonIntroDesc: A coloured square appears to the left or the right of centre. Press by COLOUR, not by place: blue is the left button, red is the right one. When colour and side agree, it is easy. When the square is on the right but the answer is on the left, your hand goes the wrong way and the answer comes out slower. That difference is the test: can you hold a rule against a habit. The classic Simon task.
sliderFeedback: Exact answer {a} · your estimate {e} · error {p}% of the scale width
sliderPlaceHint: Put the marker where the answer is
sliderPromptArea: What is the area under the graph?
sliderPromptSigned: Above is plus, below is minus. What is the signed area?
sliderReleaseHint: Let go — it counts in {n} s
slotNightDesc: Can’t sleep — breathing only, no score
solRule: Every move captures. Leave one piece
solStuck: Dead end: nothing left to capture
solitaireChessDesc: Every move is a capture, and any piece can take any other. Leave a single piece on the board without running into a dead end. 24 steps: from three pieces to ten, from easy boards to tricky ones.
sortGoalOneColour: Gather each colour into one vessel
sortHint: Pick the category this word belongs to
sortRefuseColour: A different colour is on top — not here
sortingGroupDesc: Fill containers where space runs out
sortingGroupFootnote: Both are about one scarcity: not what order to place things in, but WHERE — there are fewer free slots than items.
sortingGroupIntroDesc:
Both are about one scarcity: not what ORDER to place things in, but WHERE. In Goods Sorting a niche holds one to four items and three alike vanish; in Water Sort a layer pours only onto its own colour and only while the tube has room.

That is what separates them from Towers, where the name suggests they belong. There a move is limited by ORDER — a larger disc never sits on a smaller one — and room never runs out. Here it is the reverse: the rule is simple, but free slots are fewer than items, and almost every legal move narrows the future. The winner is not whoever finds a slot fastest, but whoever holds in mind what will be left after the move.
spanFootnote: Wechsler / Corsi paradigm. Biomarker max_span saved separately per modality — verbal vs spatial WM comparable on one Statistics screen.
spanGroupDesc: Digits or space, forward or backward
spanGroupIntroDesc:
This is not an exercise but a fork: the card opens a group of memory-span tests. Inside — digits and space, forward order and backward.

Forward order shows how many items you can hold. Backward also demands turning them over in your mind without dropping any — which is why it comes out noticeably worse. Pick the variant you want inside.
spatialGroupDesc: Turn it in your head, push it through, plot a path
spatialGroupFootnote: What they share: the move has to be worked out in your head first — on the board almost any move looks legal and leads nowhere.
spatialGroupIntroDesc: Nine exercises about space: turn things in your mind, push blocks through, plot a path. “Mental Rotation” — find the rotated copy of a cube shape. “Number Twist” — rotate a 2×2 block to put the numbers in order. “Pipe Network” — turn the pipes so water reaches every end.
spatialLabDesc: Pipes and number twist — two exercises in mental rotation
spatialLabIntroDesc: Four puzzles on one screen. “Pipe Network”: tap a pipe to select it and turn it with the “Left” and “Right” buttons below the board until water reaches every end. A double tap on a pipe or cell turns it clockwise too. “Number Twist”: tap a cell to select a 2×2 block with that cell; the same buttons turn the whole block — put the numbers in order. “Number Slide” and “Sliding Network”: tap a cell to select its row and column; the ← → arrows slide the row and ↑ ↓ the column, round and round. Your own level; the game is saved on the device.
spatialLabNetL1: Turn the one highlighted pipe — the rest are locked.
spatialLabNetL2: One pipe is turned the wrong way. Find it yourself — no hint, nothing locked.
spatialLabNetL3: Two neighbouring pipes that join each other are turned the wrong way.
spatialLabNetL4: A T-junction and the three pipes next to it are turned the wrong way.
spatialLabNetL5: Every pipe that can turn is off — rebuild the whole network.
spatialLabNetNoColour: Pipes the water has reached are not shown in colour.
spatialLabNetPatch: {w}×{w} board. Wrongly turned pipes: {a}, all in one connected patch; junctions among them: at least {j}.
spatialLabNetslideShifts: {w}×{w} board. Slides used to scramble the network: {s}.
spatialLabRulesNet: Tap a pipe to select it, then turn it with the buttons below the board or by double-tapping the pipe — clockwise. Goal: water from the source reaches every pipe, with no open end anywhere.
spatialLabRulesNetslide: Here the pipes don’t turn — they ride along with whole rows and columns: tap a cell and slide it with the ← → and ↑ ↓ arrows. The source moves with its row. Goal: water reaches every pipe with no open ends.
spatialLabRulesSixteen: Tap a cell to highlight its row and column. The ← and → arrows slide the row, ↑ and ↓ slide the column, round and round by one cell. Put the numbers in order.
spatialLabRulesTwiddle: Tap a cell to select the 2×2 block with it. The buttons below the board or a double tap turn the whole block. Put the numbers in order; the numbers themselves stay upright as the block turns.
spatialLabShiftDisplacement: {w}×{w} board. Total distance of the numbers from their places, in cells: {d}.
spatialLabShiftL1: One slide: the line is highlighted and the direction is shown.
spatialLabTwiddleBound: {w}×{w} board. Total distance of the numbers from their places, in cells: {d}. At least {m} moves.
spatialLabTwiddleExact: {w}×{w} board. Moves in the shortest solution: {n}.
spatialLabTwiddleL1: One turn: the block is already highlighted and the direction is shown.
spatialLabTwiddleL2: One turn: find the block and the direction yourself.
spatialLabTwiddleL3: Two turns of the same block — a 180° turn.
spatialLabTwiddleL4: Two turns of different blocks that overlap.
spatialLabTwiddleL5: The shortest solution is three moves, and the blocks share numbers.
spatialLabTwiddleNoColour: Numbers already in place are not shown in colour.
spatialNetDesc: Rotate the pipes so water reaches every end
spatialSpanIntroDesc: CANTAB-style: a grid where squares light up in random order. Reproduce the sequence IN REVERSE. Length grows until you fail twice at the same length. Backward variant — purer test of visuospatial working memory than forward (requires mental rearrangement).
spatialTwiddleDesc: Rotate a 2×2 block and put the numbers in order
sprintReadyHint: {n} seconds — solve as many as you can
sprintResultWin: Level cleared: {correct} correct, {score} points, best streak {streak}
srsTypingHint: A typo blocks the way — fix it to go on
stopSignalDesc: Press Go, but stop on signal
stopSignalIntroDesc: Press Go on the green signal. But if a red signal follows — stop and do not press. A harder Go/No-Go: trains prefrontal control and suppression of already-initiated actions.
storyDesc: Read a story → recall now and after 90s
storyDistractorHint: Solve math. This is the pause before recall.
storyInfoBody: Read 30s → Math distractor 30s → Recall 1 → Math distractor 90s → Recall 2
storyIntroDesc: Logical Memory subtest (Wechsler Memory Scale) — classic episodic memory test. Read a short story (~30 sec), then distractor (arithmetic 30 sec) — immediate recall (write what you remember). Then distractor 90 sec — delayed recall. Biomarkers: immediate_recall_pct, delayed_recall_pct, retention_rate (delayed/immediate; ≥0.85 = normal). Critical for business: do you remember meeting details after 1.5 min of distraction.
storyReadAuto: Moves on by itself in {n} s
storyReadHint: Remember details — you will recall them
storyRecallHint: Write everything you remember from the story
stroop2Hint: Tap FONT COLOR · ignore word meaning
stroopDesc: Ink colour, not the word meaning
stroopEmoLangFallback: Charged words exist only in Russian and English for now — the run will use English. If you do not read it, this becomes a plain Stroop.
stroopEmoLvlParams: {n} words · {w} s to answer · {p}% emotional words
stroopEmoPass: To pass: name the ink color correctly on ≥80% of words (timeout counts as an error)
stroopEmotionalIntroDesc: Name the COLOUR the word is printed in, and do not read the word itself. The words come in three kinds: alarming, pleasant and plain. On the alarming ones your hand slows down by itself, even though the meaning has nothing to do with the task — and that involuntary delay is exactly what the game catches. The emotional version of the Stroop task.
stroopHintInk: Tap the button with the INK colour
stroopHintWord: Tap the button with the word MEANING
stroopIntroDesc: The word "RED" is painted blue — tap "blue". Trains cognitive control and inhibition of automatic responses.
stroopLvlParams: {n} trials · {w} s response window · {p}% conflict trials
submarinesDesc: A fleet is hidden somewhere at sea. Tap a cell to fire: a dot is a miss, red is a hit, dark means the ship is sunk. Ships are straight and never overlap, but may stand side by side. Sink the whole fleet before you run out of shots: you get slightly more than a smart bot needs on the same fleet. Each level the sea gets bigger, the fleet larger and the shots fewer.
sudokuBaseRule: Base: each digit 1–{n} exactly once per row, column and box.
sudokuDesc: Digits with no repeats in each row, column and box (6×6 and 9×9)
sudokuEx_antiking: The blue 3 is placed. Diagonally touching red cells cannot hold another 3.
sudokuEx_antiknight: The blue 3 is placed. Red cells (an “L”, like a knight moves) cannot hold another 3.
sudokuEx_arrow: Example: the circle shows 8, the arrow holds 3 and 5 — they sum to the circle.
sudokuEx_diagonal: Yellow cells are the two diagonals. A second 3 on the same diagonal (red) is not allowed.
sudokuEx_evenodd: Example: a □ cell holds 2, 4, 6 or 8. A ○ cell holds 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
sudokuEx_hyper: The yellow square is an extra 3×3 zone (the real board has four). Digits cannot repeat inside it.
sudokuEx_jigsaw: Instead of square boxes — irregular regions. Each region holds 1–9 with no repeats.
sudokuEx_killer: Example: a 2-cell cage marked “7” — its digits sum to 7 and don’t repeat (e.g. 3 and 4).
sudokuEx_kropki: Example: 2 ⚫ 4 — black dot, one is double. 4 ⚪ 5 — white dot, differ by 1. No dot — neither.
sudokuEx_nonconsec: Cells next to a 3 cannot hold 2 or 4 (consecutive digits).
sudokuEx_sandwich: Example: in a row 1·3·5·9·… the edge clue is 8, because 3+5 sit between the 1 and the 9.
sudokuEx_thermo: Example: along a thermometer 2 → 4 → 7 — each digit is strictly larger than the previous.
sudokuEx_thermocage: Example: a thermometer runs 2 → 4 → 7 from the bulb, while a 2-cell cage marked “9” holds two different digits summing to 9 (4 and 5). A cell can sit on a thermometer and inside a cage at once — then both rules apply together, and that is what narrows it to a single digit.
sudokuEx_towers: Example: a “1” at the edge — the first building is the tallest and hides the rest. A “6” — the row strictly rises: 1·2·3·4·5·6.
sudokuEx_unequal: Example: a chain a < b < c in a row. Cell a cannot hold 8 or 9 — two larger digits must fit after it. The chain cuts options before any cell is filled.
sudokuFractalDeepIntroDesc: A sudoku nested in a sudoku up to three layers deep. Dive through the dashed cells to the very bottom and solve there: digits float up layer by layer. Finish the root grid to win. The game saves itself.
sudokuFreeHubDesc: Classic, no variants: pick size and difficulty
sudokuGroupFootnote: All three share one rule: a digit never repeats in a row, a column or a box. What differs is the board. Each keeps its own level count and its own history — games are never mixed.
sudokuGroupIntroDesc:
This is not an exercise but a fork: the card opens three boards of one puzzle. The rule is the same in all of them — a digit never repeats in a row, a column or a box.

The classic board climbs a ladder: levels bring variant rules, and the difficulty road sets how hard a technique each step demands. Samurai and fractal are long forms that live for hours: samurai has five grids sharing corner blocks, while in the fractal one the answer of a nested grid becomes the digit in the cell above. Pick a board inside.
sudokuIntroDesc:
Fill the grid so digits appear exactly once in every row, column and block. The classic logic puzzle.

🎚 Levels — new variant rules unlock as you climb:
• L9 ⟍ diagonals: digits are also unique on both diagonals
• L14 ♞ anti-knight: equal digits cannot be a knight move apart
• L18 ⊞ hyper: 4 extra 3×3 zones with no repeats
• L22 ≠ non-consecutive: side-neighbours cannot differ by 1
• L26 ♚ anti-king: equal digits cannot touch even diagonally
• L30 ◩ even/odd: □ cell = even digit, ○ = odd
• L34 ● kropki: a white dot means neighbours differ by 1, a black one means double
• L38 ⊐ sandwich: the number at the edge is the sum of digits between 1 and 9 in that line
• L42 🌡 thermometers: digits increase along the thermometer, from the bulb
• L46 ↗ arrows: the digit in the circle is the sum of digits along the arrow
• L50 🌡+ thermo and cages: two rules at once — the chain grows from the bulb, the cage adds up to its corner
• L54 ◆ ALS belt: singles and pairs no longer carry you — almost locked groups do
• L62 ⧉ jigsaw: irregular blocks instead of squares
• L66 ⛓ chains belt: the move is found along a chain — if 5 here, then not there
• L80 ★ legend board: the hardest in the bank, one for the whole ladder
• L81 ✚ combo: two rules at once — thermo with anti-knight, sandwich with parity, cages with diagonals

👑 Killer — the grid splits into cages: digits in a cage add up to the number in its corner and never repeat.

🆓 Free — a 6×6 or 9×9 board with no variants, your choice of difficulty.
sudokuKillerHubDesc: Cage sums in the corners, no repeats inside a cage
sudokuKillerRule: Killer: the board is split into cages. Digits in a cage sum to its clue and don’t repeat inside it.
sudokuLessonUnavailable: No other board at this difficulty is available for a separate lesson.
sudokuPracticeOnly: Practice attempt — no level or rating increase.
sudokuRuleAntiking: Equal digits cannot touch even diagonally (a king’s move).
sudokuRuleAntiknight: Equal digits cannot be a knight’s move apart.
sudokuRuleArgyle: Eight short diagonals of the diamond pattern are dashed: digits never repeat along any of them.
sudokuRuleArrow: Digits along the arrow sum to the number in the circle. They may repeat: an arrow adds up, it does not forbid equal digits — the ban still applies only within a row, column and box.
sudokuRuleBetween: Digits on the line lie strictly between the digits in the circles at its ends.
sudokuRuleDiagonal: Digits are also unique along both diagonals.
sudokuRuleEvenodd: □ even, ○ odd — the shape hints each cell’s parity.
sudokuRuleHyper: Four extra 3×3 regions also hold 1–9 with no repeats.
sudokuRuleJigsaw: Blocks are irregular, not squares — each still holds 1–9.
sudokuRuleKillerdiag: Two rules at once: inside a tinted cage digits add up to its corner number without repeating, and each digit appears once on both main diagonals.
sudokuRuleKropki: White dot between cells: consecutive (±1). Black dot: one is double the other.
sudokuRuleLittlekiller: A number with an arrow outside the grid is the sum of the digits along the diagonal it points to. Digits may repeat along that diagonal.
sudokuRuleLockout: Digits in the diamonds at the ends differ by at least 4; line digits are neither equal to them nor between them.
sudokuRuleNonconsec: Orthogonally adjacent cells cannot differ by 1.
sudokuRulePalindrome: A grey line reads the same from both ends: digits at equal distance from the ends match.
sudokuRuleRegionsum: Blue line: in every box it passes through, its digits add up to the same total.
sudokuRuleRenban: Digits on a purple line form a consecutive run in any order, with no repeats.
sudokuRuleSandparity: Two rules at once: an edge number is the sum of digits between 1 and 9 in that line, and cell marks fix parity (square — even, circle — odd).
sudokuRuleSandwich: Find the 1 and the 9 in the line. Add up the digits squeezed BETWEEN them — that is the edge number. The 1 and 9 themselves do not count. A zero means the 1 and 9 sit side by side. Tap an edge number and I will explain that exact one.
sudokuRuleThermo: Digits strictly increase along each thermometer from the bulb.
sudokuRuleThermocage: Two rules at once: digits strictly increase along each thermometer from the bulb, and inside a tinted cage they add up to its corner number without repeating.
sudokuRuleThermoknight: Two rules at once: digits strictly increase along each thermometer from the bulb, and equal digits never sit a chess knight’s move apart.
sudokuRuleTowers: Each digit is a building height. An edge number says how many buildings are visible from that side: a building is visible when it is taller than everything before it.
sudokuRuleUnequal: A sign between two cells compares their digits: the point aims at the smaller one. Signs join into chains — a chain tells you more than a single pair.
sudokuRuleWhisper: Neighbouring digits on a green line differ by at least 5.
sudokuRuleXsums: A number at the edge of a row or column is the sum of the first X digits from that side, where X is the first of those digits (it counts too).
sudokuRuleXv: X between cells means they sum to 10, V means 5. All are shown: unmarked neighbours never sum to 5 or 10.
sudokuTowersHubDesc: Edge clues: how many buildings you can see
sudokuUnequalHubDesc: Signs between cells, chains of comparisons
sudokuWhyNotLocal: This digit does not clash with its neighbours directly — but another one belongs here. Look at the whole row, column and box.
suiteArrowsDesc: One arrow, two buttons: flankers, position, number of choices or a cue
suiteDecisionsDesc: Nobody states the rule — you infer it from wins and losses
suiteInhibitionDesc: Don't press the forbidden one, and cancel a move already started
suitePositionsDesc: Remember WHERE it lit: a whole pattern, a chain of blocks, a chain in reverse
suiteStreamDesc: A stream with no breaks: hold a rare target, hold a rule that keeps changing
suiteStroopDesc: Colour argues with meaning: ink vs word, ink vs emotion
switchTopBadgeHint: The top badge tells WHAT to judge now. Left / right button.
switchingTaskIntroDesc: You see a pair like "3A". The cue on top says what to judge: the digit — odd or even, or the letter — vowel or consonant. The task changes without warning, so watch the cue. Right after a change the answer always comes out slower than when the task repeats — and that delay is what is being measured here.
tapNodeToReplay: Tap a completed node to replay it and earn more stars
targetsIntroDesc:
Coloured shapes flash at the bottom. There are TWO modes and the task differs — switch them on the settings screen.
"Field": a target is when two of the three shapes share a colour. See it, press it; all colours different, hands off.
"Joker": a target is when the colour of the circle from the PREVIOUS round turns up among the shapes. You have to hold it in mind, so this one tests memory one step back as well as speed.
The costly mistake is not being late but pressing on nothing: those presses are what the game counts.
teachAllWordsFamily: The “{piece}” family: keep the start, change the ending — “{word}”. Words in this family: {n}.
teachAllWordsLook: There are {total} words on the wheel. {n} of them share their start with another word: find those as families. The biggest family starts with “{piece}”.
teachAllWordsSingle: “{word}” has no relatives by its start — look for it on its own, letter by letter.
teachAnagramEnd: The ending is left — “{piece}”. {n} of the {total} words end like that: endings come in few varieties, so you check them last — and they confirm the word best.
teachAnagramLook: Look at the letters first. The rarest one here is “{piece}”: only {n} of the {total} words this length contain it. Start from it — a rare letter narrows the search more than any other.
teachAnagramMiddle: Add the middle two letters at a time — “{piece}”. Holding a pair in mind is easier than trying letters one by one.
teachAnagramStart: Place the beginning — “{piece}”. {n} of the {total} words this length start like that: a familiar opening is recognised faster than a whole word.
teachBankAverage: A roll brings three or four cells on average. But a one — one chance in six — burns everything unbanked.
teachBankRace: Watch your opponent too: if they are almost home, caution will not save you — take more risk. If you are far ahead, bank more often.
teachBankRule: Weigh the risk: unbanked progress divided by six. While less than 15–20 is unbanked, the average gain beats the average loss — rolling pays.
teachBartPlan: Every pump adds points, but a burst wipes the whole round. Decide BEFORE the round how many pumps you will take, and stick to that number.
teachBartScout: Where a balloon bursts is learned only by trying: the first balloons are scouting, not earning. The mean burst point grows with the level, so revise your number instead of guessing it.
teachBondsTen: Keep the complements to ten in mind — 3+7, 4+6, 2+8. Most pairs come together through them rather than through scanning every number.
teachChessBlindChunks: Remember in chunks, not square by square: a pawn chain, a king behind its pawns, a rook on an open file. The positions come from real games, so chunks are always there.
teachChessBlindCount: First a sum to check. Hold the position as a picture, not by reciting it: your head is busy with numbers.
teachChessBlindMove: Move {n}: {piece} {from} → {to}. Update the picture in your head: {from} is now empty, the piece stands on {to}.
teachChessBlindMoved: On {sq}: {piece}. It arrived with move {n}. Answer by the piece’s last move, not by the first picture.
teachChessBlindStayed: On {sq}: {piece}. It has stood there since the position was shown; no move touched it.
teachCorsiBackward: In reverse mode do not flip it point by point on the fly. First build the route forwards, as it was shown, then walk it from the end when you answer.
teachCorsiEyes: Follow every flash with your eyes and do not look away until the display ends. One missed flash breaks the whole route — after that it is guessing.
teachCorsiPath: Memorise not the blocks one by one but the PATH the flashes trace: run an imaginary line through them. Five flashes become one route — a zigzag, a letter, a hook.
teachCountGroups: Up to four dots are seen as a number, without counting. Split the cluster into groups of three or four and add the groups — that is what “without counting” means.
teachCrossFirst: Start with the word that crosses the most — “{word}”: it has {n} crossings and opens a letter in {n} words.
teachCrossLook: The grid holds {total} words, and they cross: every word you find opens letters in its neighbours. So the order matters more than speed.
teachCrossNext: {n} of {total} letters are already open here: {piece}. The more is open, the fewer options — “{word}”.
teachDictChunk: Piece {i}: “{c}”. Say it to yourself — then type it.
teachDictDone: Write it the same way: hear it whole → split it into pieces → dictate to yourself piece by piece.
teachDictIntro: A whole phrase will not stay in your head — you dictate it to yourself in pieces. Hear it all, split it into pieces of two or three words, type piece by piece.
teachDictListen: First listen to the whole phrase without typing anything.
teachDictStuck: Stuck on a character? Replay the phrase instead of trying letters: the input will not move until the character is right.
teachEchoConsonant: “{v}” — a consonant is swapped: {b} instead of {a}. Rule it out.
teachEchoDone: Answer the same way: follow the sounds in order and rule out any option where even one spot does not match.
teachEchoDouble: “{v}” — an extra sound: {b} instead of {a}. Rule it out.
teachEchoIntro: A pseudoword cannot be guessed from meaning — you can only hear it sound by sound, left to right. The traps differ from it in one spot.
teachEchoListen: Listen: keep the sounds in order in your head, not the overall impression.
teachEchoPick: That leaves “{w}” — that is what was said.
teachEchoSwap: “{v}” — neighbouring sounds are switched: {b} instead of {a}. Rule it out.
teachEchoVowel: “{v}” — a vowel is swapped: {b} instead of {a}. Rule it out.
teachFacesNoFeature: no single feature sets this one apart — hold on to the name and the fact
teachFindConjunction: There are two kinds of distractors — name them silently (“blue stars, yellow circles”). The odd one fits neither name: it has the colour of one kind and the shape of the other.
teachFindOneTrait: The mix gets in the way: pick ONE trait — shape or size — and compare only by it, ignore the rest. The odd one is the one that matches nobody in that trait.
teachFindPopout: Don’t search one by one: take in the whole board. If the odd one differs in colour, it pops out by itself — your eye finds it before you start checking.
teachFmAttraction: Lure an enemy piece, most often the king, onto a bad square — usually with a sacrifice — and punish it on the next move.
teachFmBackRankMate: The king behind its own pawns is locked on the back rank. A rook or queen on that rank — and there is nowhere to go.
teachFmDeflection: A defender guards a key square or piece. Deflect it — force it away, and what it guarded falls.
teachFmDiscoveredAttack: Your piece blocks the line of a long-range piece. Move it away with a threat — and a second attack is revealed.
teachFmDoubleCheck: Check by two pieces at once: it cannot be blocked or captured — the king can only move.
teachFmEdge: Result: a decisive advantage — material is still level, but the opponent’s position collapses.
teachFmFork: One piece attacks two at once. Find a square from which your piece hits two valuable targets — the opponent can save only one.
teachFmHangingPiece: Look for an enemy piece that nobody defends: you can simply take it. Check every capture — what attacks and who defends.
teachFmMateIn1: Look at the enemy king: which squares around it are free and who controls them. Mate is a check that cannot be escaped, blocked or captured.
teachFmMateIn2: Mate in two: the first move leaves no defence — often a check or a sacrifice. After any reply, mate follows next move.
teachFmPin: An enemy piece stands on a line in front of a more valuable one — the king or queen. Attack it: it cannot move away.
teachFmSkewer: A valuable piece stands on a line in front of a less valuable one. Strike along the line: the valuable one steps aside and exposes the one behind.
teachFmTrappedPiece: An enemy piece has no safe retreat. Attack it — and it is lost.
teachGoodsCap: From level eighteen the niches differ in size: some hold two, some hold four. A third good will not fit a two-slot niche, while a four-slot one keeps a free space after a triple — read the capacity, not the look.
teachGoodsFree: Clear a niche COMPLETELY. Half-empty niches choke the board: there are moves aplenty, yet nowhere to build a triple.
teachGoodsNoPath: No solution to show here — let us go through the rule instead.
teachGoodsTriple: THREE identical goods in one niche disappear — not two, and not a pair from different niches. Every move brings a good to a niche where it will be the third.
teachGoodsWhyFree: The niche is now completely empty — that is the room for the next triple.
teachGoodsWhyRoom: Take the top good off to reach the one you need underneath.
teachGoodsWhyStack: Place it with its own kind: the good waits for a third instead of taking someone else’s room.
teachGoodsWhyTriple: A third of the same kind — the triple clears and the niche frees up.
teachHiddenHalf: Ask “{q}”: yes for {yes}, no for {no}. The best question splits those left closest to half: either answer removes half of them.
teachHiddenLast: One is left — that is the hidden one. Pick them and press “That’s the one!”.
teachIowaSwitch: Sample every deck several times before settling. Penalties are rare, and two draws cannot tell a good deck from a ruinous one.
teachIowaTotal: Track the NET result per deck over recent draws, not the wins. A deck with big rewards and bigger penalties is a losing deck, even right after a big win.
teachKidsSortAgain: The rule changes more than once: after a run of ✓, a new ✗ means it has switched again. Back to colour, then to shape again.
teachKidsSortRule: First sort by colour: a red card goes to the red circle, a blue one to the blue square. Shape does not matter yet.
teachKidsSortShape: Then try sorting by shape: circle to circle, square to square. When the ✓ come back, you have found the rule — stick to it.
teachKidsSortSwitch: The rule can change without warning. The sign: a ✗ where the same kind of card was right a moment ago.
teachKqQDone: Every row is filled and no queen attacks another — solved.
teachKqQOnly: Row {row}: only one free square is left — {cell}. Place it.
teachKqQOnlySafe: Row {row}: {k} free squares, but only {cell} avoids a dead end — the others cut off a later row.
teachKqQRule: A queen attacks its row, its column and both diagonals. You need {n} queens, so exactly one in every row and every column. Start with the row that has the fewest free squares: that is where you have the least choice.
teachKqQSafe: Row {row}: of {k} free squares we take {cell} — a solution still exists from here.
teachKqTDone: Every square is visited — the tour is complete.
teachKqTForced: Jump {n}: {cell}. This square has only one exit left. Skip it now and later you can only enter it as a dead end.
teachKqTOnly: Jump {n}: {cell} — there is no other jump.
teachKqTRest: From here on, the same rule to the end: each time, go where there are the fewest exits.
teachKqTRule: The knight moves in an L: two squares straight and one to the side. You must visit {cells} squares. The key technique is Warnsdorff’s rule: jump where you will have the fewest exits afterwards. Edges and corners go first, while you can still reach them.
teachKqTSafe: Jump {n}: {cell} — a tour still exists from here.
teachKqTWarnsdorff: Jump {n}: {cell} — it has the fewest exits ({k}). Warnsdorff’s rule: take the hard squares while there is still a way in.
teachLogicAllAgree: Every remaining option agrees here — so that is the answer.
teachLogicClueFull: The number is already reached — the clue's other cells get nothing.
teachLogicClueNeedsAll: The clue needs exactly as many as there are free cells left — so all of them are taken.
teachLogicConnect: Otherwise part of the board would be cut off.
teachLogicNoShortLoop: Otherwise a loop would close where it must not.
teachLogicOnlyPlace: There is nowhere else for it — only here.
teachLogicPair: These cells are linked: knowing one gives the other.
teachLogicRuleOut: Ruled out: this option would break a rule.
teachLogicTrial: No simple technique gets this: the solver had to try options here.
teachLspanOrder: The words are spoken one by one and never shown. Tap the ones you heard in the same order: the first word heard goes first.
teachLspanOrderMiss: The right words in the wrong order count as a mistake, and the round ends at once. One mistake per game is allowed.
teachLspanSimilar: Later on, look-alike words appear next to the ones you heard. Tap the word you heard, not the one that sounds like it.
teachMahjongCount: With four identical free tiles, take any pair. With only two, first check whether another pair opens more: what you remove does not come back.
teachMahjongFree: A tile is free when nothing covers it from above AND at least one side — left or right — is clear. Neither colour nor layer matters by itself.
teachMahjongPair: Here is a pair you can take right now. Take the UPPER tiles first: each of them holds the ones below, and removing it opens several moves at once.
teachMathRound: Round, then correct: 7×48 is 7×50 minus 7×2. There is no time for long multiplication, and the correction is almost always a single step.
teachMatrixShape: Memorise the SHAPE the cells form — a letter, a corner, a line — instead of each cell. One shape instead of seven addresses.
teachMissingCheck: Go over the table and check your triples: whose triple is absent is the missing one. Choose by the triple, not by “looks like”.
teachMissingName: Name each one silently by three traits: “red, round, two eyes”. Memory holds a whole picture badly, but three words well.
teachMnemoChain: Bind “{a}” and “{b}” into one scene: let the first act on the second. The order then holds by itself.
teachMnemoChainWords: “{a}” → “{b}”: one scene where the first does something to the second. The more absurd, the stronger.
teachMnemoDone: Play it the same way: turn them into images, chain them, then walk the chain in order.
teachMnemoIntroNumbers: Bare digits do not stick. The technique: turn each number into a WORD by its consonants, then chain the words. Let us work through the first {n}; the rest go the same way.
teachMnemoIntroNumbersNoPegs: Bare digits do not stick: bind them into scenes two or three at a time instead of repeating the row. There is no peg table for this language yet.
teachMnemoIntroWords: A row of {n} words holds together not by counting “first, second” but by a CHAIN of scenes: each next word does something to the previous one.
teachMnemoOrder: You answer IN ORDER, which is why the chain matters: recall the first scene and it pulls the second. The row has {n}.
teachMnemoPegFirst: {n} is “{word}” ({why}). The consonants make the word: vowels are free, so any of them fit.
teachMnemoWordFirst: The first word is “{b}”. Picture it as an object in a concrete place, not as text.
teachNavigatorHome: Keep a running total of the shift: how many cells you went right or left and up or down in all. Home lies opposite that sum: 2 right and 1 up means home is down and to the left — “South-west”.
teachNavigatorRoute: Say the route as arrows — “up, right, right, down”: a chain is easier to hold than a picture. If the map is rotated, rotate the arrows with it.
teachNavigatorTurns: A turn is counted from the direction of travel, not from the screen: picture yourself facing forward. Going up and turning right on screen is “Right”; going down and turning right on screen is already “Left”.
teachNbackDepth: In 2-back keep the last two squares in mind and shift them like a tape: compare each new one with the square two steps back.
teachNbackLure: A trap: the square repeats the previous one, not the one N back. It looks like a match, but it is not — do not press.
teachNbackMatch: A match is the same square that lit up N steps back. In 1-back compare with the previous one: same square — press.
teachOspanOrder: The equation is there to block rehearsal. Finish it COMPLETELY, then bring the letters back: darting between the two erases both.
teachPairsCheck: Check it backwards: seeing “{b}”, does “{a}” come up? If not, the picture was weak — make it brighter instead of repeating the words.
teachPairsDone: Play it the same way: one vivid scene per pair, then check it backwards.
teachPairsIntro: A word pair sticks through ONE picture where both words act together, not through repetition. Let us work through a few of these {n} pairs.
teachPairsLink: {a} and {b}. One scene again, and let it be absurd: the absurd sticks, the ordinary fades.
teachPairsLinkFirst: {a} and {b}. Put them in one scene: not side by side but interacting — one doing something to the other.
teachPairsMatch: Then the words are shuffled and you match the pairs. Match by the picture, not by the list: the picture brings the second word back.
teachPalaceBack: Backwards is the same road from the end: {place} — {item}. The technique works both ways, which is why the game asks for it.
teachPalaceDone: Play it the same way: place the objects, then walk the route forward and back.
teachPalaceIntro: The memory palace: {n} places along a familiar route, one object on each. Later you recall the walk, not the list.
teachPalaceLink: Place {n} — {place}. Here: {item}. Again one picture, with the object right ON the place, not beside it.
teachPalaceLinkFirst: Place 1 — {place}. Put {item} here. Tie them with ONE picture and make it odd: the ordinary fades, the absurd sticks.
teachPalaceRecall: {place} — what is here? {item}. If the picture was vivid, the answer comes on its own.
teachPalaceWalk: Now walk the route. The order of places is the order of objects — follow the road, not a list.
teachPatternPeriod: First check for REPETITION: does a block come round again? If not, look at the DIFFERENCES between neighbours, and only then at the differences of those.
teachPhAnswerSpot: That was “{w}” — the differing spot had {dx}.
teachPhAnswerVowel: That was “{w}” — the difference was in the vowel.
teachPhDone: Answer the same way: know where the pair splits, and listen only to that spot.
teachPhIntro: The two words differ in ONE sound. Find where they split and listen only to that spot — the rest is shared.
teachPhProbe: Now you will hear one of the two. Listen only to the spot where they differ.
teachPhSpot: “{a}” and “{b}” split in one spot: {da} versus {db}. Listen to both.
teachPhVowel: “{a}” and “{b}” differ only in the vowel in the middle, and the spelling is a poor guide here. Listen to both.
teachPicturePairsGroup: With triples and quads, keep EVERY place of one picture in mind: a group clears only when all its cards are opened in a row.
teachPicturePairsPlaces: While the cards are face up, tie each picture to a place: corners, edges, middle. Then open where you saw its twin, not at random.
teachPicturePairsSwap: From level 22, after a mistake face-down cards swap places and the pair lights up. Move the picture in your memory to where its card went.
teachPrlNoise: One failure is not a rule change: even the right colour sometimes pays nothing. Switch after two or three failures in a row, not after the first.
teachQueueDoor: 🚪 marks the front of the queue: the animal at the door stands first.
teachQueueFirst: First in the queue is the animal no arrow points to: nobody has to be ahead of it.
teachQueueGlued: 🔗: this animal stands right behind the one that has just taken its place.
teachQueueNext: Next comes an animal whose clues are all met: everyone who must be ahead of it is already in the queue.
teachQueueThink: Several animals fit this spot by its clues. Try each in your head: the wrong one runs into a clue further down the queue.
teachRingCorner: The corners are already set: {piece}. {n} bank words fit this pattern — “{word}”.
teachRingFirst: Start with a rare first letter: only {n} of these words begin with “{piece}”. It is “{word}”.
teachRingLook: The bank makes {total} five-letter words, but there are only four sides. Each corner is a letter shared by two words: find one word and it hints at its neighbours.
teachRmetCompare: “{word}” would look like this: {cues}. Compare it with these eyes.
teachRmetCues: Eyes first, words later. What you can see here: {hint}.
teachRmetDone: Answer the same way: read the eye cues → compare with the neighbouring words → pick the one closest to the cues.
teachRmetEyes: Look at the EYES — lids, brows, direction of gaze — not at “the face” in general. The options are deliberately close in meaning, so compare them with each other rather than with your first impression.
teachRmetPick: The cues “{hint}” fit “{word}” best — that is the answer.
teachRotationAnchor: Do not rotate the whole figure — pick ONE landmark (a tail, a notch, a corner) and watch where it goes. Comparing one point is faster than a whole outline.
teachRpEven: The gaps between the beats are equal — tap just as evenly, neither rushing nor dragging.
teachRpHigher: The second note is higher than the first — the line goes up.
teachRpListen: Listen to the row. Beats in it: {n}.
teachRpListenTones: Listen to the notes in a row. There are {n} here.
teachRpLower: The second note is lower than the first — the line goes down.
teachRpPitchDone: Answer the same way: listen to where the line goes from the first note — up or down.
teachRpPitchIntro: Compare each note with the one before: higher or lower? Keep the line in your head, not the notes themselves.
teachRpRhythmDone: Play it the same way: catch the tempo and hold it instead of counting beats.
teachRpRhythmIntro: Hold the TEMPO, not the count: the beats come evenly, like steps. Repeat the pattern at the same pace.
teachRpTap: First beat right away, then keep the same pace. Listen once more and tap along in your head.
teachRspanJudge: Read the sentence and decide whether it makes sense. Remember its last word: you will be asked for it at the end.
teachRspanNonsense: Nonsense is an answer too: tap Nonsense, but still remember the last word.
teachRspanRecall: After the set, type the last words in the same order, separated by spaces.
teachRunArches: Answer arches: solve the problem first, then look at the arches. The options differ by 1, 2 or 10 — check the last digit and the tens.
teachRunBridge: Bridge and gap: pick your lane early — you can only change it before the span begins. Miss the bridge and you fall, and the run is over.
teachRunColumns: At a pole, add up both stacks and take the bigger sum — the first number of a stack often misleads. Choose your side before the pole: you cannot cross it.
teachRunGuard: Guardian: at the finish your number must be at least the guardian’s. Every miss and every red costs you, so protect your number to the end.
teachRunMiddle: Your number takes what its middle runs over, not what its edges brush. To take several blues from one row, slide sideways right through them and steer around the reds.
teachRunPile: A pile instead of digits: count the full frames of ten and the cells in the part-filled one — 4 frames and 7 cells make 47. A frame is two columns of five, so you see how many are filled and how many are empty at a glance, without counting.
teachRunRamp: Ramp: drive onto the green pad — the jump carries you over the big red and over the gap. Blues on the far side are bait: after them you will not make it to the pad.
teachRunWalls: A wall across the road: take the smaller minus. “×2” beats “+N” only if your number is already bigger than N.
teachRunnerGates: Look at BOTH shown signs: they tell the direction — up or down — and the number–letter alternation. The next one continues exactly that pair, not the habitual “plus one”.
teachRunnerWindows: Don’t count the shapes: keep ONE feature of the target in mind — the shape, or the shape AND the colour when the target is a pair — and sweep the windows for that feature. A shape with a red dot is a decoy.
teachScholarsContinue: Next {move}: the attack on the king goes on without a pause.
teachScholarsDefend: Defence {move}: after it there is no mate in one, and no piece is given away.
teachScholarsDefendThreat: First find the threat: the opponent threatens mate with {move}.
teachScholarsKing: Look at the enemy king: which squares around it are blocked by its own pieces, and what already attacks nearby.
teachScholarsMate: {move} is mate: a check with no defence. The king has nowhere to go, the attacker cannot be taken, nothing can block.
teachScholarsSacrifice: Sacrifice {move}: give up a piece to open the king.
teachScholarsThreatAsk: Is mate threatened? Hand the move to your opponent in your head and check: do they have mate in one?
teachScholarsThreatNo: No: none of the opponent’s moves gives mate.
teachScholarsThreatYes: Yes: if it were their move, {move} would be mate.
teachSchulteCenter: Hold your gaze at the CENTRE and search with peripheral vision. Darting from cell to cell is reading the table — that trains reading speed, not span.
teachSliderAnchor: Place the mark from ANCHORS, not from the edge: the midpoint, the quarters, the tenths. “Just past a third” is more accurate than trying to measure an absolute distance.
teachSolLast: Move {n}: {move}. One piece is left — solved.
teachSolLoneTarget: Move {n}: {move}. Only this piece can reach that one — take it while the hunter is still on the board.
teachSolOnlyCapture: Move {n}: {move}. There is no other capture on the board.
teachSolOnlySafe: Move {n}: {move}. There are other captures, but only this one avoids a dead end.
teachSolPlan: Solve from the end: the last one standing will be the {piece} — it makes the most captures. Take a piece that only one hunter can reach while that hunter is still alive.
teachSolRule: There is one rule: every move is a capture. There are no colours, any piece can take any other, a pawn captures diagonally upwards. The goal is to leave one piece. A dead end is more than one piece and nothing to capture.
teachSolSafe: Move {n}: {move}. After this capture a solution still exists.
teachSolSurvivor: Move {n}: {move}. The capture goes to the piece that will remain last: pile the captures on it.
teachSpanBackward: Do not memorise the reversed order separately: learn the row as usual and reverse it when answering, group by group from the end.
teachSpanChunks: Memory holds four CHUNKS, not nine digits. Break the row into groups of three or four — “729 · 418” — and say them in a rhythm, like a phone number.
teachSpatialSpanPath: The cells are not a set of points but a LINE. Join them into a path: a five-node trajectory holds better than five separate places.
teachSubFinish: Hit? Finish it: first the four neighbours, and once a second hit shows the direction — only along that line. A ship is straight and never turns off its line.
teachSubHeat: Fire where a living ship can stand in the most ways. The picture shows the board as the bot sees it: the redder the cell, the more ships could be there.
teachSubParity: Fire in a checkerboard pattern — every other cell. The shortest ship covers two cells, so the checkerboard cannot miss it: half the shots for the search.
teachSudokuHiddenBox: In this box the digit {d} has only one place left — here.
teachSudokuHiddenCol: In column {n} the digit {d} has only one place left — here.
teachSudokuHiddenRow: In row {n} the digit {d} has only one place left — here.
teachSudokuNaked: Only {d} fits this cell: every other digit already appears in its row, column or box.
teachSudokuPlain: This cell is {d}. No simple technique gets it — from here it takes case analysis.
teachTrackerGroup: Do not jump from target to target — hold them as ONE SHAPE, the vertices of a single polygon. Four trajectories cannot be held; one changing quadrilateral can.
teachTrafficFirst: Look at the cars between the red car and the exit: they must go. For each, ask what stops it from moving — and untangle the chain from its far end.
teachTrafficNext: The next move frees a cell for whoever blocks the exit. Move a car exactly as far as needed, without blocking the others.
teachTrailA: Look for the next number ahead of time: while you draw the line to “3”, your eyes already find “4”. Searching while moving is where the time is won.
teachTrailB: Hold the pair in mind, not two separate counts: “1 — A, 2 — B, 3 — C”. Say it aloud — then switching from number to letter won’t throw you off.
teachTraitCheck: Before checking, scan the field again row by row: did you miss anyone or mark someone extra?
teachTraitMark: Has {trait} — mark it and move along the row.
teachTraitNot: First find everyone with {trait}, then DROP those with {trait2}. Mark only the ones left.
teachTraitPair: Two traits at once: first find everyone with {trait}, then among them mark those with {trait2}. Holding both traits in mind at once is slower and error-prone.
teachTraitScan: Look at one trait only — {trait}. Ignore the rest: colour, shape and eyes get in the way if you track everything at once.
teachWcstHold: One success does not confirm the hypothesis: the card may have matched two features at once. Keep the rule while it keeps working.
teachWcstHypothesis: The rule is hidden and cannot be guessed from one card. Hold ONE hypothesis — say “I am sorting by colour” — and test it with your next move.
teachWcstSwitch: An error here is not noise but a signal: the feature has changed. Cycle through them — colour, shape, number — instead of guessing.
teachZhDone: Answer the same way: hear the syllable, picture its line — level, up, dip or down.
teachZhIntro: Listen not to the syllable but to how the voice MOVES. One syllable in four tones is four different words.
teachZhPair23: Tones 2 and 3 are easy to mix up: both end by rising. The difference is at the start: {a} {pa} goes up right away, {b} {pb} first goes down.
teachZhTone1: Tone 1 — {zh} {py}: the voice stays high and level, like a held note.
teachZhTone2: Tone 2 — {zh} {py}: the voice rises, as in a puzzled “huh?”.
teachZhTone3: Tone 3 — {zh} {py}: the voice dips and rises a little — the lowest of the four.
teachZhTone4: Tone 4 — {zh} {py}: the voice drops sharply from high to low, like a curt “no!”.
tolFailedPreset: {e} extra moves with a limit of {r} — round not cleared
tolWonPreset: Round cleared: {e} extra moves out of {r}
towerLondonIntroDesc: Top: goal arrangement. Bottom: current arrangement. Move balls between pegs (tap source peg, then target peg). Pegs have different capacities. Solve in MINIMUM moves. Trains planning and inhibition of premature action.
trafficJamDesc: Slide the cars along their own axis and get the red car to the exit on the right. Cars cannot pass through each other. One move is one car sliding any number of cells; the counter shows moves / minimum.
trailCrossOk: Lines may cross — order and speed are what count
trailMakingIntroDesc: Tap the circles in order or slide your finger across them. Connect numbers and letters in order as fast as possible. Version B (number-letter-number switching) is a standard test of cognitive flexibility.
trailPass: To pass: finish the trail within {t}s with at most {e} errors
transferProgressHint: Achievements and levels live on this device. Export a code here, paste it on another device.
trkResultFail: {hits} of {total} correct, {extra} extra — level not cleared
updAvailableBody: A new version is out — download now?
updLatest: You are on the latest version
visualSearchDesc: Find all the target shapes among similar ones
visualSearchIntroDesc: Tap the shapes in the field that match the sample. The field is filled with similar shapes at various angles. Find all the target shapes — the reference is shown alongside. The target changes every round, and as levels rise there are more objects and targets. A classic selective-attention paradigm.
vocabSrsHint: Pick the translation of the word above
vocabSrsIntroDesc: The core of vocabulary learning — spaced repetition (SM-2, Anki-style). A quiz: word → 4 translation options. Miss it and the card returns today; get it and it moves out 1 → 3 → 7+ days, right before you would forget. Grading is automatic: a fast correct answer pushes the interval further. Add your own course words as “word = translation”. Progress is tracked per language pair.
voiceMissing: No voice for this language found on the device — audio will not play. Pick another language.
voiceMissingLang: No voice for “{lang}” found on this device. Pick another language.
voiceSoundOff: Sound is off, and this exercise speaks. Turn sound on in settings.
vsFindAll: Find all of these shapes — in any rotation
vsFindConj: Find the shape with this colour and form
waterSortDesc: Pour the colours until each tube holds just one
waterSortHiddenHint: Hidden layer: a “?” is revealed by a move
waterSortIntroDesc: Tap a tube to lift its top run, tap another to pour. You may only pour onto the same colour or into an empty tube, and only while there is room. The level is done when every tube is empty or full of one colour. Think ahead about where the colour in your way will go: there are only two free tubes.
wcstHint: Which reference card matches? (rule is hidden)
wcstIntroDesc: Bottom: a card. Top: 4 reference cards. Sort by a HIDDEN rule: colour, shape, or count. The rule is learned only from ✓/✗ feedback. After a run of correct answers the rule silently changes. ⚠️ The first pick after a change can't be guessed — an error here is NORMAL: that's exactly how you find the new rule. The classic Wisconsin Card Sort.
wcstLvlParams: {n} trials · rule switches after {s} in a row
wcstPass: To pass: repeat the old rule after a switch no more than {c} times, and ≥55% correct
wcstRuleShifted: ↻ The rule just changed — this error was unavoidable, that is how you find the new one
wordPairsIntroDesc: Memorize connections between words, then restore the pairs. Trains associative memory — the ability to link information together.
wordsGroupDesc: Vocabulary and pulling a word out of memory
wordsGroupFootnote: From recognising a word to pulling it out unaided — in order of effort.
wordsGroupIntroDesc:
Six vocabulary exercises, from recognition to retrieval. Spotting a word in a list is easy: the answer is in front of you. Recalling it unaided is different work — and that is what carries fluent speech.

Inside the hub they run in order of effort: spaced repetition, sorting by meaning, the missing word in a phrase, word-or-not decisions, anagrams, and finally fluency — as many words with one letter as you can in a minute.
